docs.title: Project Aegis
docs.text:
Standalone guardrail library for A2A agent executors.

Aegis provides two composable guardrail primitives — Guard and MutationGuard — with a fluent .use() API. Drop them into any A2A executor to validate inputs and sanitize outputs without coupling your agent logic to guardrail implementation details.

Aegis ships the engine, a set of built-in validators, and the validator contract. Use the built-ins (see Validators), or write your own by satisfying a small protocol (or subclassing BaseValidator / BaseMutationValidator) — see Custom Validators.

docs.title: Why Aegis?
docs.text:
Every A2A executor that handles user input or produces output needs guardrails. The alternative is implementing checks manually in each executor. Here's why a library is better:

The core reason to run guardrails as separate validators — rather than embedding instructions in your agent's system prompt — is reliability. Prompt instructions are suggestions; under adversarial pressure (prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, multi-turn escalation), a model can ignore them. Separate validators enforce independently, outside the agent's context window, and cannot be talked out of doing their job.

Beyond that:

DIY Approach Aegis Checks written inline, duplicated per executor Validators written once, reused across any executor or agent architecture No standard for what "fail" means PassedResult / FailedResult with consistent error codes and details Concurrency wiring left to the developer Concurrent execution handled automatically via asyncio.gather() No spans on validation calls OpenTelemetry span written for every validation, automatically Ad-hoc error handling per check Centralized on_fail — LOG, EXCEPTION, NOOP, or custom callable Detection and mutation logic tangled together Guard for detection, MutationGuard for mutation — clean separation Guardrail policy mixed into agent business logic Guards are defined and composed independently — policy changes don't touch agent code

For a deeper treatment of why standalone validators outperform prompt-embedded instructions on reliability, reusability, testability, and cost, see Why Separate Validators?

docs.title: Guard — Concurrent Detection
docs.text:
All validators run in parallel. No values are modified. Returns a GuardResult you inspect to decide what to do.

BlockTopic and MaxLength below are validators you write — subclass BaseValidator (see Custom Validators):

from aegis import Guard, OnFailAction

input_guard = (
    Guard("input-guard")
    .use(BlockTopic("fraud"), on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION)
    .use(MaxLength(5000))
)

result = await input_guard.validate(value=user_message)
if result.has_failures:
    for failure in result.failures:
        print(f"{failure.validator_name}: {failure.error_message}")

docs.title: MutationGuard — Sequential Mutation Pipeline
docs.text:
Validators run in order. When one fails, its mutate() is called and the corrected value is passed to the next validator. Returns a MutationGuardResult with the final output.

from aegis import MutationGuard

output_guard = (
    MutationGuard("output-guard")
    .use(EmailRedactor())
    .use(ToneNormalizer())
)

result = await output_guard.validate(agent_response)
final_response = result.output if result.was_mutated else agent_response   # str in → output is a str

docs.title: Aegis: a2a-sdk v0.3 → v1.0 migration
docs.text: Scope note: Aegis is a server-side wrapper library. It wraps AgentExecutor, EventQueue, and RequestContext, and transforms Part/Message/Artifact objects. It builds no servers, clients, or AgentCards. So most of the upstream migration guide does not touch Aegis code — it touches your consumers' apps. This doc separates the two.

docs.title: TL;DR — what actually breaks Aegis
docs.text:
Two changes account for ~all the work:

  1. Pydantic → Protobuf types. Part(root=TextPart(...)), part.root, isinstance(part.root, TextPart), and every .model_copy(update=...) call stop working. This is the core of _utils.py, plus clones in context.py and event_queue.py.
  2. a2a.utils → a2a.helpers, and new_agent_text_message no longer exists.

Everything else (enum renames, one import move) is mechanical. AgentCard, server setup, client, and push-notification changes do not apply to Aegis — see the "Not Aegis's problem" section so you can tell consumers what they must change.

docs.title: 1. Blast radius by file
docs.text: File What breaks Severity src/aegis/a2a/_utils.py part.root, isinstance(part.root, TextPart), Part(root=...), part.root.model_copy(...), import TextPart High — core projection layer src/aegis/a2a/event_queue.py Part(root=TextPart(...)), event.model_copy, event.artifact.model_copy, import TextPart High src/aegis/a2a/context.py context.message.model_copy(...), from a2a.utils import get_message_text High src/aegis/a2a/executor.py from a2a.utils import new_agent_text_message, new_task, TaskState.rejected, TaskUpdater args Medium pyproject.toml version pin a2a-sdk>=0.3.20,<0.4 trivial tests/** Part(root=TextPart(...)), Role.user, TaskState.*, FilePart/DataPart/FileWithBytes mechanical, high volume

docs.title: 2. The Part/Message model change (the hard part)
v0.3 (Pydantic RootModel union)
docs.text:
from a2a.types import Part, TextPart
Part(root=TextPart(text="hi"))           # wrap, then access via .root
isinstance(part.root, TextPart)          # discriminate by wrapper type
part.root.text                           # read text
part.root.model_copy(update={"text": x}) # copy via Pydantic

docs.title: v1.0 (Protobuf flat union)
docs.text:
from a2a.types import Part
Part(text="hi")                          # flat — no wrapper, no .root
part.HasField("text")                    # discriminate via HasField()
part.text                                # read text
# copy: protobuf has no model_copy — see below

docs.title: Concrete rewrites
docs.text:
_utils.py :: build_view — the type discriminator changes from isinstance to HasField: 

# v0.3
items = [
    ContentItem(id=_part_id(i), type=ContentType.TEXT, value=part.root.text)
    for i, part in enumerate(parts) if isinstance(part.root, TextPart)
]
# v1.0
items = [
    ContentItem(id=_part_id(i), type=ContentType.TEXT, value=part.text)
    for i, part in enumerate(parts) if part.HasField("text")
]

_utils.py :: apply_view — the copy-with-update. Protobuf has no model_copy. Options (pick one, verify against the shipped SDK): 

# Option A — copy the proto, mutate the field in place (protobuf idiom)
def _copy_with_text(part, text):
    new = type(part)()
    new.CopyFrom(part)
    new.text = text
    return new
# Option B — if a2a.helpers exposes a Part text constructor, rebuild:
#   Part(text=text)   # only safe when the part carries nothing but text
build_view/apply_view only ever address text parts today and preserve non-text parts untouched. Option B (Part(text=...)) looks viable because of that, but prefer Option A (CopyFrom): Aegis is slated to support file/data parts in future, and Option B silently drops any sibling field on the part (metadata, and eventually file/data payloads on mixed parts). CopyFrom-then-mutate is future-proof; Part(text=...) bakes in the text-only assumption you're planning to remove. Verify against the real v1.0 Part proto before committing — this is the one place the upstream guide is thin on server-side detail.

event_queue.py 

# v0.3
parts = [Part(root=TextPart(text=resolved))]                              # line ~197
return event.model_copy(update={"artifact":
        event.artifact.model_copy(update={"parts": parts})})              # line ~164
# v1.0
parts = [Part(text=resolved)]
new = type(event)(); new.CopyFrom(event)
del new.artifact.parts[:]; new.artifact.parts.extend(parts)               # proto repeated-field write
return new

context.py 

# v0.3
self._guarded_message = context.message.model_copy(update={"parts": mutated_parts})
# v1.0
msg = type(context.message)(); msg.CopyFrom(context.message)
del msg.parts[:]; msg.parts.extend(mutated_parts)
self._guarded_message = msg

These CopyFrom + repeated-field patterns are protobuf standard. The exact field names (parts, artifact, text) should match the v1.0 protos; confirm once against the installed package.

docs.title: 3. Helper / util import moves
docs.text:
v0.3 v1.0 Used in from a2a.utils import get_message_text from a2a.helpers import get_message_text context.py:5 from a2a.utils import new_task from a2a.helpers import new_task executor.py:11, tests from a2a.utils import new_agent_text_message removed — use new_message / new_text_message executor.py:11,381

new_agent_text_message has no drop-in replacement. v0.3 signature was new_agent_text_message(text, context_id, task_id). In v1.0: 

from a2a.helpers import new_message   # role defaults to ROLE_AGENT
# was: new_agent_text_message(error_message, task.context_id, task.id)
# now (verify param names against helpers signature):
new_message([Part(text=error_message)], task_id=task.id, context_id=task.context_id)
# or new_text_message(text=error_message, ...) if it accepts task/context ids

docs.title: 4. Enum renames (mechanical)
docs.text:
Only two enums are used in Aegis: TaskState and Role.

v0.3 v1.0 TaskState.rejected TaskState.TASK_STATE_REJECTED TaskState.completed TaskState.TASK_STATE_COMPLETED Role.user Role.ROLE_USER Role.agent Role.ROLE_AGENT

Locations: executor.py:381 (TaskState.rejected); tests use TaskState.completed/rejected and Role.user throughout tests/integration/* and tests/unit/test_guarded_context.py.

docs.title: 5. Server-internal types — VERIFY, not covered by upstream guide
docs.text:
The upstream guide documents the client and app-setup surface. Aegis lives on server internals the guide barely mentions. Confirm these still exist / same shape in v1.0 before trusting the migration:

  • a2a.server.agent_execution.RequestContext — Aegis subclasses it and reads ._params, .task_id, .context_id, .current_task, .related_tasks, .call_context, .message. GuardedContext is the biggest risk if the base constructor signature changed.
  • a2a.server.events.{Event, EventQueue} — GuardedEventQueue proxies these.
  • a2a.server.tasks.TaskUpdater(event_queue, task_id, context_id) and .update_status(state, message, final=True) — used in _reject_task.
  • TaskArtifactUpdateEvent, Artifact, Task, TaskStatusUpdateEvent field access (event.artifact.parts, task.context_id, task.id).

The client guide shows StreamResponse wrapping artifact_update/status_update on the client side; server-side event types may keep their own shape. Don't assume — check the installed a2a.server.events.

docs.title: 6. Not Aegis's problem (tell your consumers)
docs.text:
These upstream v1.0 changes are app-level — Aegis never touches them, but your docs/examples/README should point consumers at the upstream guide for:

  • DefaultRequestHandler(..., agent_card=...) now required
  • A2AStarletteApplication etc. removed → create_jsonrpc_routes() / create_rest_routes() / create_agent_card_routes()
  • AgentCard restructure (supported_interfaces, AgentInterface, modes moved)
  • create_client() replaces A2AClient/ClientFactory
  • send_message() returns AsyncIterator[StreamResponse]
  • ClientConfig.push_notification_config singular
  • v0.3 compat flag (enable_v0_3_compat=True) if consumers run mixed fleets

docs/getting-started.md, docs/installation.md, and docs/a2a-wrapper.md likely show consumer app setup — audit those for the removed wrapper classes.

docs.title: 7. Backward compatibility — supporting both SDKs from one Aegis
docs.text: Two different "v0.3 compat" ideas — don't conflate them: - Upstream enable_v0_3_compat=True (§6) = a v1.0 server accepting v0.3 wire clients. App-level. Not aegis. Consumers set it on their route factories. - This section = aegis-the-library working whether the installed a2a-sdk is 0.3 or 1.0, so existing 0.3 agents don't break when Aegis adds 1.0 support. This is the one that matters for a library shipped to many agents.

docs.title: Why a single codebase can support both
docs.text:
Aegis's entire version-sensitive surface is ~6 primitive operations, and they're already funneled through one seam (build_view/apply_view + two clones). Everything else — the speculative executor, the holdback buffer, config dataclasses — is version-agnostic and doesn't change. Isolate those 6 primitives behind a compat module and the rest of Aegis never imports a version-specific symbol.

Critical constraint: Aegis src must not do top-level from a2a.types import TextPart anywhere — that import fails to load on v1.0 (the type is gone). All version-specific imports move into _compat.py.

docs.title: The shim: src/aegis/a2a/_compat.py
docs.text:
Detect the version once with EAFP import guards (more robust than parsing the version string — handles pre-releases/forks):

# src/aegis/a2a/_compat.py
from __future__ import annotations
from a2a.types import Part

try:
    # v0.3: wrapper types exist
    from a2a.types import TextPart
    _V03 = True
except ImportError:
    TextPart = None            # type: ignore
    _V03 = False

if _V03:
    def is_text_part(part) -> bool:            return isinstance(part.root, TextPart)
    def part_text(part) -> str:                return part.root.text
    def make_text_part(text: str) -> Part:     return Part(root=TextPart(text=text))
    def copy_text_part(part, text: str) -> Part:
        return Part(root=part.root.model_copy(update={"text": text}))
    def copy_with_parts(obj, parts):           return obj.model_copy(update={"parts": parts})
    def copy_artifact_event(event, parts):
        return event.model_copy(update={"artifact": event.artifact.model_copy(update={"parts": parts})})
    from a2a.types import TaskState
    TASK_STATE_REJECTED = TaskState.rejected
    from a2a.utils import get_message_text, new_task, new_agent_text_message
else:
    def is_text_part(part) -> bool:            return part.HasField("text")
    def part_text(part) -> str:                return part.text
    def make_text_part(text: str) -> Part:     return Part(text=text)
    def copy_text_part(part, text: str) -> Part:
        new = type(part)(); new.CopyFrom(part); new.text = text; return new
    def copy_with_parts(obj, parts):
        new = type(obj)(); new.CopyFrom(obj)
        del new.parts[:]; new.parts.extend(parts); return new
    def copy_artifact_event(event, parts):
        new = type(event)(); new.CopyFrom(event)
        del new.artifact.parts[:]; new.artifact.parts.extend(parts); return new
    from a2a.types import TaskState
    TASK_STATE_REJECTED = TaskState.TASK_STATE_REJECTED
    from a2a.helpers import get_message_text, new_task
    from a2a.helpers import new_message as _new_message
    def new_agent_text_message(text, context_id=None, task_id=None):
        return _new_message([Part(text=text)], task_id=task_id, context_id=context_id)

Then the seam files import from the shim instead of a2a directly:

  • _utils.py: build_view uses is_text_part/part_text; apply_view uses copy_text_part.
  • event_queue.py: Part(root=TextPart(...)) → make_text_part(...); the event.model_copy(...) line → copy_artifact_event(event, parts).
  • context.py: context.message.model_copy(...) → copy_with_parts(msg, parts); get_message_text from shim.
  • executor.py: new_task/new_agent_text_message/TASK_STATE_REJECTED from shim.

Future data-type support: Aegis handles only text parts today, but file/data parts are on the roadmap. When they land, the shim is the natural extension point — add is_file_part/part_file/make_data_part etc. alongside the text primitives, version-branched the same way. Keep the text-only Part(text=...) shortcut out of copy_text_part (use CopyFrom, per §2) so mixed parts carrying both text and a payload don't lose data once non-text support arrives. build_view/apply_view will grow to project non-text ContentItem types, but the seam stays the seam.

GuardedContext's base-class construction (§5) is the one thing a shim can't fully paper over if the RequestContext.__init__ signature diverged between versions — verify that constructor on both SDKs; if it differs, the shim needs a build_request_context(...) primitive too.

docs.title: Declaring the dependency
docs.text:
Keep the pin wide, not split: 

# pyproject.toml — one package, both majors
dependencies = ["a2a-sdk>=0.3.20,<2"]
Add a CI matrix testing against a2a-sdk==0.3.* and a2a-sdk==1.* so the shim can't silently rot on one side. The full test suite already exercises the seam — run it twice, once per pinned major.

docs.title: When to drop it
docs.text:
The shim is deliberate, tracked debt. Remove the _V03 branch (and widen the pin to >=1.0.0,<2) once your fleet's 0.3 agents have migrated — the code collapses back to the v1.0-only forms in §2–4. Mark it:

# TODO: dual-SDK shim — delete the _V03 branch once no consumer pins a2a-sdk <1.0

docs.title: Alternatives (if the shim's runtime branching bothers you)
docs.text:
• Optional extras — aegis[a2a03] vs aegis[a2a1] with version-gated pins. Simpler code, but consumers must pick the right extra; the import-time branch problem (top-level TextPart import) still forces a _compat.py anyway.
  • Major-version split — Aegis 1.x → a2a 0.3, Aegis 2.x → a2a 1.0. Cleanest code (no branching), but two maintenance lines and consumers must bump Aegis in lockstep. Only worth it if the shim surface grows well past these 6 primitives.

Recommendation: the shim. The surface is tiny and already isolated; one package that "just works" on both is the least friction for a fleet mid-migration.

docs.title: 8. Suggested migration order
docs.text:
1. Bump pin: a2a-sdk>=1.0.0,<2 in pyproject.toml; uv sync. Let imports fail loudly.
  2. Fix _utils.py first (build_view/apply_view) — everything routes through it. Nail the Part copy semantics (§2) and keep the Part cardinality guarantee.
  3. Fix context.py and event_queue.py clones (CopyFrom + repeated fields).
  4. Fix executor.py imports/enums/new_agent_text_message.
  5. Update helper imports repo-wide (a2a.utils → a2a.helpers).
  6. Migrate tests mechanically (Part(root=TextPart) → Part(text=), enum renames, FilePart/DataPart → flat Part(file=)/Part(data=)).
  7. Run the suite. The integration tests in tests/integration/test_a2a_pipeline.py and test_guarded_* are the real acceptance gate.

Unverified assumptions flagged above (§2 Part copy, §5 server internals) are the only places this could go sideways — resolve those against the installed SDK first.

docs.title: 9. As-built — verified against a2a-sdk 1.1.2
docs.text: Everything above §9 was written speculatively (hence the "verify against the installed SDK" caveats). This section records what the migration actually took once run against the real SDK. Where §9 conflicts with §1–§8, §9 wins.

docs.title: Shape shipped: dual-SDK shim (§7), lock pinned to 1.x
docs.text:
• src/aegis/a2a/_compat.py — the shim. pyproject.toml stays a2a-sdk>=0.3.20,<2; uv.lock pins 1.1.2, so the default dev/CI environment is v1.
  • tests/_a2a_compat.py — a test-side twin (version-agnostic object builders/readers) so the whole suite runs on both majors. pythonpath = ["tests"] in the pytest config lets tests/unit/ and tests/integration/ do from _a2a_compat import .... It is a helper module, not a test case — hence it lives at the tests/ root, not in a subfolder.
  • CI: the suite runs in a dedicated test workflow with two legs — the primary job runs on the locked 1.x environment with coverage; a second job pins a2a-sdk==0.3.* as a pass/fail-only 0.3 leg so the shim can't silently rot on the 0.3 side.

docs.title: Corrections — the guide got these wrong
docs.text: Guide said Reality on 1.1.2 §3: from a2a.helpers import new_task (drop-in) Wrong. v1 new_task(task_id, context_id, state, ...) is a different function. The 0.3 new_task(message) equivalent is new_task_from_user_message(message). §2/§5: TaskUpdater.update_status(state, msg, final=True) final was removed (v1 sig: update_status(state, message, timestamp, metadata)), and TaskStatusUpdateEvent has no final field. Use TaskUpdater.reject(message) for the reject path — it exists in both majors with the same signature, so no shim branch is needed. §5: GuardedContext base ctor is "the biggest risk" Non-issue. RequestContext.__init__ did change (v1 requires call_context; request is now SendMessageRequest), but GuardedContext already passes everything by keyword incl. call_context, and the _params instance attr exists in both majors. No change needed. §2: discriminate via part.HasField("text") Correct for text. But HasField("file") raises — v1 Part has no file oneof member (its fields: text, raw, url, data, filename, media_type). File parts do not map 1:1 from 0.3.

docs.title: Additions — SDK changes the guide didn't cover
docs.text:
• MessageSendParams → SendMessageRequest. v1 removed MessageSendParams; RequestContext(request=...) now takes a SendMessageRequest (fields: tenant, message, configuration, metadata). Any test/harness that builds a context must branch on this.
  • Data-part construction. Part(data={...}) fails on v1 — the data field is a google.protobuf.Value, not a dict/Struct. Build via Part(data=Value(struct_value=...)) and read via dict(part.data.struct_value).
  • Protobuf copy semantics. Assigning a sub-message (SendMessageRequest(message=m)) copies it — there is no shared reference as on Pydantic 0.3. Identity assertions (x is original_msg) that passed on 0.3 fail on protobuf; assert against the object the context exposes (ctx.message) or on content, not on the external input object.
  • EventQueue() construction deprecated on 1.x — see below.
  • v1 is real and stable — 1.0.0 … 1.1.2 are published; this migration is verified against 1.1.2, not a pre-release.

docs.title: EventQueue() direct instantiation — deprecated on 1.x (owned test subclass)
docs.text:
v1 makes a2a.server.events.EventQueue an abstract producer interface. Constructing EventQueue() directly emits a DeprecationWarning and redirects to EventQueueLegacy; its docstring states "executors should accept it and not construct one" and warns that both the redirect and EventQueueLegacy "will be removed in a future release." It offers two sanctioned ways to run an executor outside the framework: "write a custom subclass or use EventQueueLegacy (deprecated)."

  • Shipped Aegis is unaffected — permanently. Aegis is an executor wrapper: it accepts the framework-provided event_queue and wraps it in GuardedEventQueue; it never constructs an EventQueue. (grep 'EventQueue(' src/ → none — only type annotations.) No consumer hits this warning through aegis.
  • Only the test suite triggered it, because tests run an executor outside the framework and need a real queue to feed execute() and read events back — exactly the deprecated path.
  • Decision: own a concrete subclass in the shim. tests/_a2a_compat.py::OwnedEventQueue is a ~15-line EventQueue subclass (the docstring's first sanctioned path). It implements only what the suite exercises: the producer enqueue_event, the close/is_closed that GuardedEventQueue delegates to the wrapped queue, and dequeue_nowait to read events back. event_queue() returns it and dequeue() takes it, so the type checker enforces that only this queue is drained, with no unchecked cast. This is warning-free and depends on neither EventQueueLegacy (whose eventual removal would otherwise break test collection at import time, even under the a2a-sdk<2 pin) nor any third-party queue internals. It works unchanged on both majors (EventQueue exists in each), and replaces the earlier dequeue_event(no_wait=True) branch the 0.3 drain path used. The ~100 DeprecationWarnings are gone, not silenced with a filterwarnings ignore.

docs.title: A2A Wrapper
docs.text:
The A2A wrapper provides two integration paths that eliminate guardrail boilerplate from your A2A agent executors. Both produce identical runtime behaviour — choose the pattern that fits your architecture.

  1. GuardedAgentExecutor — wraps any existing AgentExecutor instance (composition)
  2. @guarded decorator — decorates any AgentExecutor class

Your execute() method stays unchanged. The wrapper sits around it, applying guards transparently via wrapped context and event queue.

A2A Server
  → GuardedAgentExecutor.execute(context, event_queue)
       ├─ Input pipeline  (Guard → MutationGuard, or reversed with mutation_first=True)
       ├─ Wrap context  → GuardedContext  (mutated input transparently accessible)
       ├─ Wrap event_queue → GuardedEventQueue  (output guards on artifacts)
       └─ inner_executor.execute(guarded_context, guarded_event_queue)
            └─ Your normal execute() code — unchanged

docs.title: Config Objects
docs.text:
Both GuardedAgentExecutor and @guarded accept InputGuardConfig and OutputGuardConfig objects that group the guard, mutation guard, pipeline order, and failure hook for each phase.

from aegis.a2a import InputGuardConfig, OutputGuardConfig

docs.title: InputGuardConfig
docs.text: Field Type Default Purpose guard Guard | None None Detection guard — validators run concurrently, no mutation mutation_guard MutationGuard | None None Mutation guard — validators run sequentially, transforms the value mutation_first bool False When True, run MutationGuard before Guard on_fail InputFailHook | None None Hook fired when the guard has failures history_provider HistoryProvider | None None Async callable returning prior conversation turns. See Conversation history below. speculative bool False Run the detection guard in parallel with the agent, buffering output until it passes. See Speculative holdback below. stream_lifecycle_events bool False When speculating, forward non-content lifecycle events immediately instead of buffering them. See Speculative holdback.

docs.title: OutputGuardConfig
docs.text: Field Type Default Purpose guard Guard | None None Detection guard on outbound artifact parts mutation_guard MutationGuard | None None Mutation guard on outbound artifact parts mutation_first bool False When True, run MutationGuard before Guard on_fail OutputFailHook | None None Hook fired when the output guard has failures artifact_filter ArtifactFilter None Predicate to select which artifacts are guarded

docs.title: Pipeline order
docs.text: mutation_first Pipeline False (default) Guard → MutationGuard — check first, then sanitize True MutationGuard → Guard — sanitize first, then check the clean content

docs.title: GuardedAgentExecutor
docs.text:
Wrap any AgentExecutor instance:

ContentFilter below is a built-in validator; MaxLength and PIIRedactor are custom ones you write against the contract. Aegis ships built-in validators (see Validators) and lets you add your own (see Custom Validators).

from aegis import Guard, MutationGuard, OnFailAction
from aegis.a2a import GuardedAgentExecutor, InputGuardConfig, OutputGuardConfig
from aegis.validators.detection import ContentFilter
from my_validators import MaxLength, PIIRedactor  # your own validators
from agent_config import BLOCKED_TOPICS

guarded_executor = GuardedAgentExecutor(
    executor=MyAgentExecutor(),
    input_config=InputGuardConfig(
        guard=(
            Guard("input")
            .use(MaxLength(5000), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
            .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
        ),
        on_fail="I'm unable to help with that request.",
    ),
    output_config=OutputGuardConfig(
        mutation_guard=MutationGuard("output").use(PIIRedactor()),
    ),
)

# Register guarded_executor with the A2A server instead of the raw executor
Parameter Type Purpose executor AgentExecutor The inner executor to wrap input_config InputGuardConfig | None Input phase configuration output_config OutputGuardConfig | None Output phase configuration

docs.title: @guarded Decorator
docs.text:
Same config objects, class-level syntax:

from aegis.a2a import guarded, InputGuardConfig, OutputGuardConfig

@guarded(
    input_config=InputGuardConfig(
        guard=(
            Guard("input")
            .use(MaxLength(5000), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
            .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
        ),
        on_fail="I'm unable to help with that request.",
    ),
    output_config=OutputGuardConfig(
        mutation_guard=MutationGuard("output").use(PIIRedactor()),
    ),
)
class MyAgentExecutor(AgentExecutor):
    async def execute(self, context: RequestContext, event_queue: EventQueue) -> None:
        query = context.get_user_input()  # mutated input if mutation_guard was set
        # ... your logic unchanged ...

Note

Pass on_fail inside the config object. Class-level on_input_fail / on_output_fail methods are not supported — put the hook in InputGuardConfig(on_fail=...) instead.

docs.title: on_fail Hooks
docs.text: on_fail is set inside the config object for each phase. It fires after guard.validate() returns with failures (not on mutation — MutationGuard always runs silently).

docs.title: Input on_fail
docs.text:
Callable signature: (failures: list[FailedResult], context: RequestContext, event_queue: EventQueue)

Value / return Behaviour True Reject the task with all failure messages joined by "; " str Reject the task with this custom message False Continue execution — explicit opt-in to allow through None (implicit return) Same as True — fail-close default

The wrapper handles task rejection automatically (a rejected terminal status + message). The hook only decides whether to reject and optionally what message to use.

# Static: reject with custom message
InputGuardConfig(guard=guard, on_fail="Your request cannot be processed.")

# Static: reject with aggregated validator errors
InputGuardConfig(guard=guard, on_fail=True)

# Callable: conditionally allow through
async def reject_on_multiple(failures, context, event_queue):
    if len(failures) >= 2:
        return True   # reject
    return False      # allow through — must be explicit

InputGuardConfig(guard=guard, on_fail=reject_on_multiple)

docs.title: Output on_fail
docs.text:
Callable signature: (failures: list[FailedResult])

Value / return Behaviour True Suppress the artifact — do not emit it str Replace artifact content with this message before emitting False Emit the artifact as-is — explicit opt-in to allow through None (implicit return) Same as True — fail-close default 
# Static: suppress the artifact
OutputGuardConfig(guard=guard, on_fail=True)

# Static: replace with a safe message
OutputGuardConfig(guard=guard, on_fail="This content has been redacted.")

# Callable: log but allow through
def log_and_continue(failures):
    logger.warning("Output issues: %s", failures)
    return False  # must be explicit

OutputGuardConfig(guard=guard, on_fail=log_and_continue)

Multiple artifacts

Each add_artifact() call is guarded independently. If two artifacts fail, the hook is called once per artifact. If you need different behaviour per artifact, manage state externally via a closure.

docs.title: Artifact Filtering
docs.text:
By default, output guards run on every TaskArtifactUpdateEvent. Use artifact_filter to selectively guard only certain artifacts — skipping metadata, sources, or debug artifacts that would cause false positives or waste compute.

The filter is a callable that receives an Artifact and returns True (guard it) or False (pass through unmodified). Both sync and async callables are supported.

# Guard only the main response, skip metadata/sources
OutputGuardConfig(
    mutation_guard=output_guard,
    artifact_filter=lambda artifact: artifact.name == "main_response",
)

# Guard everything except specific artifacts
OutputGuardConfig(
    mutation_guard=output_guard,
    artifact_filter=lambda artifact: artifact.name not in {"sources", "debug_metadata"},
)

# Async predicate (e.g., feature flag lookup)
async def should_guard(artifact):
    if artifact.name.startswith("_internal"):
        return False
    return True

OutputGuardConfig(
    mutation_guard=output_guard,
    artifact_filter=should_guard,
)

When artifact_filter is None (the default), all artifacts are guarded — preserving backwards-compatible behaviour.

docs.title: mutation_first
docs.text:
Use mutation_first=True when you want to sanitize content before checking it — useful when guards should see the clean version rather than raw user input.

InputGuardConfig(
    guard=(
        Guard("input")
        .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
    ),
    mutation_guard=MutationGuard("sanitize").use(PIIRedactor()),
    mutation_first=True,   # redact PII first, then filter the clean input
    on_fail="I can't help with that.",
)

The same flag works on OutputGuardConfig — set mutation_first=True to sanitize output before running the output guard.

docs.title: Input Mutation and GuardedContext
docs.text:
When InputGuardConfig.mutation_guard produces a mutated value, the context passed to execute() is a GuardedContext — a RequestContext subclass that transparently provides the mutated text:

async def execute(self, context: RequestContext, event_queue: EventQueue) -> None:
    query = context.get_user_input()          # mutated text (or original if nothing changed)
    original = context.original_input         # pre-mutation text
    original_msg = context.original_message   # pre-mutation Message object

get_user_input() and message.parts both read from the same guarded Message — it is not possible to get inconsistent results.

docs.title: Output Interception
docs.text:
Output guards run inside GuardedEventQueue, which intercepts TaskArtifactUpdateEvent events. This works because TaskUpdater.add_artifact() ultimately calls event_queue.enqueue_event().

Event type Guarded? TaskArtifactUpdateEvent Yes — output guard + mutation applied TaskStatusUpdateEvent (working, completed, etc.) No — passes through Task (task creation) No — passes through

ValidationError from on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION propagates up through add_artifact(), halting execution — use this for hard stops on output violations.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
The wrapper adds parent spans around existing Guard/MutationGuard spans:

guarded_executor.execute
├─ guarded_executor.input_guard
│  └─ guard.{name}.validate          (existing Guard spans)
│     └─ validator.{name}
├─ guarded_executor.input_mutation
│  └─ mutation_guard.{name}.validate (existing MutationGuard spans)
│     └─ mutation_validator.{name}
├─ [user's execute() runs]
├─ guarded.output_guard              (per artifact event)
│  └─ guard.{name}.validate
└─ guarded.output_mutation           (per artifact event)
   └─ mutation_guard.{name}.validate

No span duplication — wrapper spans provide pipeline-level timing, existing spans provide per-validator detail. In speculative mode the guard runs under a guarded_executor.speculative span while the agent runs concurrently. See Observability for exporter setup.

docs.title: Speculative Holdback
docs.text:
Input detection guards can add noticeable latency when a validator is slow (for example, one that makes a network call). Normally they run before the agent, so every request pays that cost even though ~99% are benign.

Speculative holdback runs the guard and the agent at the same time. The agent starts immediately; its output is held in a buffer and only revealed once the guard passes. Think of it as CPU branch prediction: assume the likely branch (input is valid), do the work early, and discard it in the rare miss.

SEQUENTIAL (default):                  SPECULATIVE (speculative=True):

│ guard ═══════════╗ (~800ms)          ├─ guard ═══════════╗ (~800ms)
│                  ║                    └─ agent ───────────╫────────▶ response
│      agent ──────╨───────▶ response        └─ output ▶[BUFFER]│
                                                              released on pass
total = guard + agent                  total ≈ agent alone
  • Guard passes (~99%): the buffer is flushed → output flows to the user. The guard's latency was hidden behind the agent's own work.
  • Guard fails (~1%): the agent is cancelled and the buffer discarded. The user sees only the rejection — exactly as in sequential mode.

Key invariant: no agent output ever reaches the user before the guard passes.

InputGuardConfig(
    guard=Guard("input").use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS)),
    on_fail="I'm unable to help with that request.",
    speculative=True,
)

docs.title: When speculation applies
docs.text: Speculation is only safe when the agent gets clean input before it starts — so it requires either no input mutation_guard, or mutation_first=True (mutation runs first, then the agent and guard run concurrently on the mutated input). If you set speculative=True alongside a non-mutation_first mutation guard, Aegis silently falls back to sequential execution — detection must run before mutation in that configuration, so it can't run concurrently.

docs.title: Read-only agents only
docs.text:
Read-only agents only

Enable speculative holdback only for agents with no external side effects at any point during execution — reads, computation, and LLM calls are fine, but no database writes, no state-mutating API calls, no file writes.

Buffering hides output; it does not undo actions. The agent gets no signal for when (or whether) the guard passed, and on a failing verdict cancellation is not instant: it only lands at the agent's next await. So a write issued at any point while speculating can commit even though the request is rejected. There is no safe window for writes.

This first release therefore supports read-only agents only. Do not set speculative=True on a write-capable agent; run it sequentially instead.

docs.title: Lifecycle events vs. content
docs.text: By default (stream_lifecycle_events=False), Aegis holds everything until the guard passes — strict non-leakage: the user sees nothing (not even a "working" status) before the verdict. Set stream_lifecycle_events=True to forward non-content lifecycle events (Task creation, TaskStatusUpdateEvent) immediately for better perceived latency, while still buffering every TaskArtifactUpdateEvent (the actual answer). Enable this only when your pre-verdict lifecycle events carry no user or model content (e.g. a static status string).

docs.title: Preconditions and caveats
docs.text:
• Read-only agents only. See the warning above — the agent must have no external side effects at any point during execution.
  • Cancellation safety is required. The failure path cancels the agent mid-execution. Your agent, its LLM/graph invocation, and any clients must unwind cleanly on CancelledError.
  • Wasted compute on rejects. Speculative runs burn LLM/tool work that is discarded when the guard fails. Acceptable at ~99% benign, but real.
  • ROI is workload-dependent. The win is largest when the guard is a large fraction of a short total (light / lookup queries). On long flows where the guard is a small slice of the total, the benefit is near-zero. Enable per-agent based on profiling.

docs.title: Conversation History
docs.text: Context-aware validators can benefit from conversation history to interpret simple replies like "yes" or "no" in context. The wrapper populates GuardMetadata.conversation_history from a user-supplied history provider and passes it to every validator; validators that use context read the field, validators that don't ignore it.

docs.title: The history_provider contract
docs.text:
InputGuardConfig.history_provider is an async callable:

HistoryProvider = Callable[[RequestContext], Awaitable[list[ConversationMessage]]]
  • Return chronological messages (oldest first), each a {"role": "user" | "assistant", "content": str} dict.
  • Return [] when no history is available — do not raise.
  • Any exception is caught, logged at WARNING, and validation continues without history.
  • The provider owns truncation. Aegis does not cap the returned length.

Aegis ships no built-in providers — the backend (SAP Agent Memory, context.related_tasks, Redis, Postgres, …) is user code. Two reference implementations live in examples/:

  • examples/history_provider_related_tasks.py — reads from RequestContext.related_tasks.
  • examples/history_provider_sap_agent_memory.py — reads from SAP Agent Memory Service (requires sap-cloud-sdk).

docs.title: Example: SAP Agent Memory
docs.text:
from examples.history_provider_sap_agent_memory import make_sap_agent_memory_provider

InputGuardConfig(
    guard=guard,
    history_provider=make_sap_agent_memory_provider(
        agent_id="my-agent-id",
        invoker_id_key="user_id",
        max_messages=10,
    ),
)

docs.title: Example: related_tasks fallback
docs.text:
Requires the A2A server to populate related tasks:

# A2A server configuration
context_builder = SimpleRequestContextBuilder(
    should_populate_referred_tasks=True,
    task_store=your_task_store,
)

from examples.history_provider_related_tasks import make_related_tasks_provider

InputGuardConfig(
    guard=guard,
    history_provider=make_related_tasks_provider(max_messages=5),
)

Multi-pod deployments

related_tasks reads from the A2A server's TaskStore. The default in-memory store is per-pod — in a Kubernetes / horizontally-scaled deployment, a follow-up request routed to a different pod will find no prior tasks and the provider returns []. Either pin sessions with sticky routing, back the TaskStore with a shared store (Redis, Postgres), or use a cross-pod backend like SAP Agent Memory as the primary provider.

docs.title: Chaining providers
docs.text:
Providers are plain callables — wrap them however you want. A common pattern is SAP Agent Memory with related_tasks as fallback:

async def hybrid_provider(context):
    history = await sap_provider(context)
    return history or await related_tasks_provider(context)

InputGuardConfig(guard=guard, history_provider=hybrid_provider)

docs.title: Standalone Guard users
docs.text:
Callers of Guard.validate() outside the A2A wrapper populate metadata themselves — the history_provider field is only used by GuardedAgentExecutor:

from aegis import GuardMetadata

history = fetch_from_wherever(user_id)  # your code
await guard.validate(
    value=user_text,
    metadata=GuardMetadata(conversation_history=history),
)

docs.text:
Pure validation engine with a fluent .use() API.

All registered validators run concurrently on each validate() call. Input is a plain string or a :class:ContentView; validators receive the view (call view.render() for the flattened text). The engine never touches transport parts — adapters map parts to a view.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

Identifier for this guard (used in spans / logs).

required normalize bool | NormalizationConfig

Controls guard-side normalization applied to each content item's value once before fanning out to validators. Accepts a bool (convenience alias) or an explicit :class:NormalizationConfig. True applies the engine profile (:meth:NormalizationConfig.for_engine — NFKC-folded, variation-selector-stripped, homoglyph-mapped); False applies none; a NormalizationConfig applies exactly the strategies it declares. Validators see the canonical form; the caller's original input is never mutated and the normalized form does not escape via GuardResult. Defaults to False so multilingual inputs round-trip untouched. Enable for security-sensitive detection over untrusted input (homoglyph / Unicode-bypass protection).

docs.title: aegis.ContentView(items) dataclass
docs.text:
The whole message a validator inspects: its parts, in order.

A validator reads the parts through items (each a :class:ContentItem) or as one flattened string through :meth:render. A mutation validator then returns :class:ItemEdit values addressed by ContentItem.id, which :meth:rebuild applies to produce the mutated view.

docs.title: render()
docs.text:
Return every part's value joined by newlines, in order.

Use this when a validator reasons over the whole message at once rather than part by part — for example, matching a pattern that may span parts.

Note: parts are joined with "\n" regardless of how the transport actually separated them, so render() is for inspection, not for reconstructing the exact original wire format.

Source code in src/aegis/validators/base.py 
def render(self) -> str:
    """Return every part's value joined by newlines, in order.

    Use this when a validator reasons over the whole message at once rather
    than part by part — for example, matching a pattern that may span parts.

    Note: parts are joined with ``"\\n"`` regardless of how the transport
    actually separated them, so ``render()`` is for inspection, not for
    reconstructing the exact original wire format.
    """
    # TODO: revisit if a validator ever needs byte-exact reconstruction of
    # the original part separators.
    return "\n".join(p.value for p in self.items)

Use this when a validator works on raw text and needs it in the standard ContentView shape the rest of the pipeline expects.

@classmethod
def from_text(cls, text: str) -> ContentView:
    """Build a view holding a single TEXT item from a plain string.

    Use this when a validator works on raw text and needs it in the standard
    ``ContentView`` shape the rest of the pipeline expects.
    """
    return cls(items=(ContentItem(id="p0", type=ContentType.TEXT, value=text),))

docs.title: rebuild(edits)
docs.text:
Apply edits to this view, returning a new view with identical item count and order.

Each :class:ItemEdit replaces one item's value by id. Items that are not addressed pass through unchanged, so cardinality and order hold by construction. An edit whose id matches no item raises :class:MutationError.

Source code in src/aegis/validators/base.py 
def rebuild(self, edits: list[ItemEdit]) -> ContentView:
    """Apply ``edits`` to this view, returning a new view with identical item count and order.

    Each :class:`ItemEdit` replaces one item's ``value`` by ``id``. Items that are not
    addressed pass through unchanged, so cardinality and order hold by construction. An
    edit whose ``id`` matches no item raises :class:`MutationError`.
    """
    ids = {item.id for item in self.items}
    new_values: dict[str, str] = {}
    for edit in edits:
        if edit.id not in ids:
            raise MutationError(f"edit references unknown item: {edit.id}")
        new_values[edit.id] = edit.value  # last edit wins on a repeated id

    return ContentView(
        items=tuple(
            replace(item, value=new_values[item.id]) if item.id in new_values else item for item in self.items
        )
    )

Wraps any AgentExecutor with automatic input/output guardrails.

    ),
    output_config=OutputGuardConfig(
        mutation_guard=my_output_mutation_guard,
    ),
)

def guarded(
    input_config: InputGuardConfig | None = None,
    output_config: OutputGuardConfig | None = None,
):
    """Decorator that wraps an AgentExecutor's ``execute()`` with guardrails.

    A thin wrapper over :class:`GuardedAgentExecutor` — the decorated class's
    original ``execute()`` is preserved and called through the same guard
    pipeline as the wrapper, so there is no duplicated logic.

    Usage::

        @guarded(
            input_config=InputGuardConfig(
                guard=my_input_guard,
                on_fail="I'm unable to help with that request.",
            ),
            output_config=OutputGuardConfig(
                mutation_guard=my_output_mutation_guard,
            ),
        )
        class MyAgentExecutor(AgentExecutor):
            async def execute(self, context, event_queue):
                # original logic here — called after guards pass
                ...

    ``on_fail`` in each config accepts a **static value** or a **callable**.
    Return ``False`` explicitly to allow through; ``None`` (implicit return)
    is treated as rejection/suppression (fail-close default).
    """

    def decorator(cls):
        original_init = cls.__init__
        original_execute = cls.execute  # captured before cls.execute is replaced

        def new_init(self, *args, **kwargs):
            original_init(self, *args, **kwargs)
            self._guarded_executor = GuardedAgentExecutor(
                executor=_OriginalAdapter(self, original_execute),
                input_config=input_config,
                output_config=output_config,
            )

        async def wrapped_execute(self, context, event_queue):
            await self._guarded_executor.execute(context, event_queue)

        cls.__init__ = new_init
        cls.execute = wrapped_execute
        return cls

    return decorator

docs.title: speculative = False class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
When True, run the detection guard in parallel with the agent.

Normally the guard runs before the agent, so every request pays the guard's latency (LLM-based validators add ~0.8–2.6s). Speculative holdback starts the agent immediately while the guard validates concurrently, and holds the agent's output in a buffer until the guard passes:

  • Guard passes (~99%): the buffer is flushed to the user. The guard's latency was hidden behind the agent's own work.
  • Guard fails (~1%): the agent is cancelled and the buffer discarded — the user sees only the rejection, exactly as in sequential mode. No output ever reaches the user before the guard passes.

Only applies when the agent can start on clean input — i.e. no input mutation_guard, or mutation_first=True. If a non-mutation_first mutation guard is configured, aegis silently falls back to sequential execution (:meth:GuardedAgentExecutor._should_speculate).

Warning

Read-only agents only. Enable speculative holdback only for agents with no external side effects at any point during execution — reads, computation, and LLM calls are fine, but no database writes, no state-mutating API calls, no file writes. On a failing verdict the agent is cancelled mid-execution; buffering hides its output but cannot undo an action already taken, so a write issued while speculating may be committed even though the request was rejected. Do not set speculative=True on write-capable agents.

Cancellation safety is also required: on the failure path the agent is cancelled mid-execution, so the agent, its LLM/graph invocation, and any clients must unwind cleanly on CancelledError.

Defaults to False — existing behaviour is unchanged.

docs.title: stream_lifecycle_events = False class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
When True (and speculating), let non-content lifecycle events through the holdback buffer instead of buffering them.

The agent's first emissions are usually a Task creation event and a TaskStatusUpdateEvent (e.g. an "Analyzing your request…" status). By default (False) aegis holds everything until the guard passes — strict non-leakage: the user sees nothing, not even a "working" status, before the verdict.

Setting this True forwards those lifecycle events immediately for better perceived latency, while still buffering every TaskArtifactUpdateEvent (the actual answer). This is a deliberate, documented relaxation of strict non-leakage — enable it only when your pre-verdict lifecycle events carry no user or model content (e.g. a static status string).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Aegis has two execution modes — Guard and MutationGuard — both with the same fluent .use() API. Choose based on whether you need to detect issues or fix them.

docs.title: Guardrail Lifecycle
docs.text:
The diagram below shows the intended integration pattern for a full A2A agent request cycle.

The validators named below are illustrative — Aegis ships built-in validators (see Validators), and you can also supply your own (see Custom Validators).

Input phase:

  1. Input Guardrails (Guard) — e.g. a content filter and a PII detector run concurrently.
  2. If any fails → propagate to TaskUpdater with a rejection message and fail the task.
  3. If all pass → continue to input mutation.
  4. Input MutationGuard — e.g. a PII redactor sanitizes the incoming message before it reaches execute().

Output phase:

  1. Output Guardrails (Guard) — e.g. a prompt-leakage check on the agent's response.
  2. If fails → suppress the artifact or update TaskUpdater with an error message.
  3. If passes → continue to output mutation.
  4. Output MutationGuard — e.g. a tone normalizer rewrites the tone before the response is returned.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
These principles explain why the library behaves the way it does.

Detect, don't mutate (Guard) : Guard validators only return PassedResult or FailedResult. They never modify the input. This makes concurrent execution safe — no validator can affect another's input.

Mutation is explicit (MutationGuard) : Only MutationGuard can transform values, via validators that implement mutate(). Detection and mutation are separate concerns with different execution semantics.

No value chaining in Guard : All Guard validators receive the original input simultaneously via asyncio.gather(). A later validator cannot see an earlier validator's side effects.

On-fail handlers are void : on_fail callbacks are side-effect only — log, notify, raise. They never return a transformed value. Value transformation belongs in MutationGuard.

Validators are pluggable — built-in or your own : Aegis ships a set of built-in validators (see Validators), and the engine runs any validator satisfying a structural protocol (Validator / MutationValidator) or subclassing BaseValidator / BaseMutationValidator, so you can add your own too. Integrate explicitly via Guard/MutationGuard for full control, or use the A2A executor wrapper for a simpler drop-in experience. The underlying API stays the same either way.

Protocol-first validators : Validators satisfy a structural protocol (Validator / MutationValidator). Any class with the right methods qualifies — no forced inheritance. BaseValidator and BaseMutationValidator are opt-in convenience base classes.

docs.title: Why Separate Validators?
docs.text:
Guardrails can theoretically be embedded directly into an agent's system prompt as behavioral instructions. Aegis takes the opposite approach — all validators run as independent calls, outside the agent. Here's why.

Reliability — the primary reason : Prompt instructions are suggestions, not guarantees. Under adversarial pressure (prompt injection, jailbreak, multi-turn escalation), a model can ignore embedded instructions. A guardrail that can be bypassed has no value when it matters most. Separate validators enforce independently — a deterministic check cannot be talked out of doing its job.

Reusability : One validator definition, used by any agent that needs it. Change once, apply everywhere. Embedding guardrail logic in prompts means copying and maintaining it in every agent separately.

Testability : Each validator can be unit tested in isolation with known inputs and expected PassedResult / FailedResult outputs — without involving the full agent. Embedded validators are entangled with agent business logic and cannot be tested or benchmarked independently.

Auditability : Separate validators produce structured results: which validator fired, what it caught, and the full FailedResult with details. Embedded validators are a black box — there is no trace of why the agent did or didn't enforce a rule.

docs.title: Guard: Concurrent Detection
docs.text:
Input ──┬── Validator A ──┬── GuardResult ├── Validator B ──┤ .results └── Validator C ──┘ .has_failures .failures 

- All validators run simultaneously via `asyncio.gather()`.
- Returns `GuardResult` — inspect `has_failures` and `failures`.
- Values are **never** modified.
- Each validator gets an `on_fail` action: `LOG` (default), `EXCEPTION`, `NOOP`, or a custom callable.

```python
from aegis import Guard, OnFailAction

guard = (
    Guard("input-guard")
    .use(ValidatorA(), on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION)
    .use(ValidatorB(), on_fail=OnFailAction.LOG)
    .use(ValidatorC())  # defaults to LOG
)

result = await guard.validate(value="some input")
print(result.has_failures)   # bool
print(result.failures)       # list[FailedResult]

docs.title: MutationGuard: Sequential Mutation Pipeline
docs.text:
Input ──► Validator A ──► [mutate A] ──► Validator B ──► [mutate B] ──► output
          validate()         │            validate()         │
          FailedResult? ───────┘            FailedResult? ───────┘
  • Validators run in registration order.
  • When a validator returns FailedResult, its mutate() is called immediately.
  • The mutated value is passed to the next validator (each sees the previous output).
  • Returns MutationGuardResult:
  • was_mutated — True if any edit was applied
  • output — the final content, mirroring the input type: a str when called with a str, otherwise a ContentView (same item count and order as the input); call .render() for text
  • results — list of all ValidationResults
from aegis import MutationGuard

guard = (
    MutationGuard("output-guard")
    .use(ValidatorA())
    .use(ValidatorB())
)

result = await guard.validate("some output")
final = result.output          # always the final content — str in → str out, mutated or not
# result.was_mutated only tells you *whether* anything changed (e.g. for logging).

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
Aspect Guard MutationGuard Execution Concurrent Sequential Mutation Never When validator fails Return type GuardResult MutationGuardResult on_fail param Yes (LOG / EXCEPTION / NOOP / callable) No Typical use Input validation, compliance, scope checking Output sanitization, PII redaction, tone correction

Use Guard when you need to decide whether to proceed with a request — the content is accepted or rejected as-is.

Use MutationGuard when you want to clean up content before passing it on — the content is acceptable but needs transformation.

docs.title: Combining Both
docs.text:
A typical executor uses both: a Guard to gate input, a MutationGuard to clean output.

from aegis import Guard, MutationGuard, OnFailAction, ValidationError
from aegis.validators.detection import ContentFilter
from my_validators import MaxLength, PIIRedactor  # your own validators

# Built once, reused across requests
input_guard = (
    Guard("input")
    .use(MaxLength(5000), on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION)
    .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=["fraud"]), on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION)
)

output_guard = MutationGuard("output").use(PIIRedactor())

# In your executor:
async def execute(request, task_updater):
    try:
        await input_guard.validate(value=request.message)
    except ValidationError as e:
        await task_updater.submit(message_with_text(f"Request rejected: {e.result.error_message}"))
        await task_updater.failed()
        return

    response = await your_agent_logic(request)

    out = await output_guard.validate(response)
    final_response = out.output          # str in → str out; already the final content
    await task_updater.submit(message_with_text(final_response))
    await task_updater.complete()

See Cookbook for more integration patterns including full executor examples.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

First public release. aegis is a deterministic guardrail engine for AI systems: a Guard / MutationGuard core with a fluent .use() API, an A2A wrapper layer, optional Unicode normalization, OpenTelemetry tracing, eight stdlib-only detection validators, and one nh3-powered mutation validator.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
• Guard / MutationGuard — view-based validation engine. Guard.validate / MutationGuard.validate take a value: str | ContentView (a string becomes a single text item). Validators implement validate(view: ContentView, metadata=None) — call view.render() for the flattened text or iterate view.items. A MutationValidator is a superset of Validator and can run detect-only under Guard.
  • Result types — PassedResult and FailedResult, each carrying a details mapping. Failure details carry only safe summaries, never the raw input.
  • Mutation path — MutationValidator adds mutate(view, metadata=None, validation_failure=None) -> list[ItemEdit]. MutationGuard applies the edits and rebuilds the view, so item cardinality and order are guaranteed by the engine. MutationGuardResult carries a single output that mirrors the input type (str or ContentView). Public types: ContentView, ContentItem, ContentType, ItemEdit, MutationError.
  • GuardMetadata dataclass with fields system, tools, and conversation_history.
  • Empty guard raises — Guard.validate / MutationGuard.validate raise RuntimeError when no validators are registered; register at least one via .use().
  • Flexible on_fail handling — LOG, EXCEPTION, NOOP, or a custom callable.
  • Shared text normalization (aegis.NormalizationConfig) — one normalize() function plus a NormalizationConfig dataclass of per-strategy toggles (Unicode form, strip variation selectors, strip format characters, collapse whitespace, map homoglyphs, case-fold), used by both the engine and the detection validators. Guard(normalize=...) accepts a bool or an explicit NormalizationConfig. Pure-ASCII input skips the non-ASCII passes for speed.
  • OpenTelemetry tracing — integrated, and a no-op when no exporter is configured.

docs.title: A2A wrapper
docs.text: • GuardedAgentExecutor / GuardedEventQueue — stage build_view → validate → apply_view on input and output. A2A parts ↔ view conversion lives in aegis.a2a._utils. Non-text parts (DataPart, FilePart) are preserved in place; a partless message is a no-op. The engine itself is A2A-agnostic.

docs.title: Detection validators (stdlib-only, detect-only)
docs.text:
• PromptLeakageCheck — rejects output reproducing the system prompt, configured sensitive fragments, or canary tokens (OWASP LLM07:2025). Exact and opt-in normalized substring matching, optional difflib fuzzy matching, optional GuardMetadata.system protection, and a max_input_chars valve.
  • ContentFilter — rejects text containing any configured blocked term or phrase. Word-boundary matching by default (avoids the Scunthorpe problem) with an opt-in substring mode; optional normalization; opaque term-index reporting by default.
  • XssDetector — flags known XSS vectors (CWE-79): HTML tags, dangerous URI schemes, legacy CSS expression(), and DOM write-sinks. Scans view.render(); decodes obfuscation to a fixed point. Toggleable strip_invisible_chars / decode_obfuscation and a max_input_chars valve.
  • SqlInjectionDetector — flags known SQL-injection constructs (CWE-89): UNION SELECT, stacked queries, equal-operand tautologies, SQL comments, and time-based blind probes. High-signal, linear (no ReDoS surface). Scans view.render(); decodes obfuscation.
  • FormulaInjectionDetector — flags input that would begin a spreadsheet formula on CSV import (CWE-1236). Scans each ContentItem as one cell candidate; skips leading padding and one structural quote; names high-impact DDE/HYPERLINK shapes via formula_shape.
  • XxeDetector — flags XML External Entity constructs (CWE-611): external entities, external/inline DTDs, parameter/general-entity declarations, and XInclude. DTD handling is capability-based (flag_bare_doctype for reject-all). Scans view.render(); masks inert comment/CDATA/PI regions; decodes obfuscation.
  • LengthValidator — min/max text length validation.
  • SizeValidator — byte-size validation against a configurable limit.

docs.title: Mutation validators
docs.text: • HtmlSanitizer — detect-and-fix sanitizer reducing HTML to a safe, allowlisted subset (XSS / mutation-XSS defense), powered by nh3 (Rust ammonia/html5ever), so it resists syntactic obfuscation. validate flags parts differing from their sanitized form with DISALLOWED_HTML; mutate returns the sanitized form per changed part. Safe defaults (HTML-only, URL schemes tightened to {http, https, mailto}, inline CSS disabled) with widening knobs. Runs under MutationGuard, or Guard for detect-only.

docs.title: Custom Validators
docs.text:
This page is the contract reference: what a validator must implement to run under Guard or MutationGuard. It applies equally whether you write a validator for your own application or contribute one to aegis.

Validators in Aegis are protocol-based: any class with the right methods qualifies. No inheritance required. BaseValidator and BaseMutationValidator are optional convenience base classes — they provide a default name property and enforce the interface via ABC, but you can satisfy the protocol directly without subclassing anything.

Contributing a validator to the repo?

This page covers what to implement. For where the code, tests, and docs live, how a validator is registered, and the release workflow, see the Authoring Guide.

docs.title: Detection vs. Mutation: the rule
docs.text:
A validator's category is a security decision, not a convenience choice. Decide it before you write any code:

  • Security concerns are detection-only. A validator that exists to stop an attack — prompt/instruction injection, SQL/command injection, XXE, SSRF payloads — must only detect and reject the request. It runs under Guard, and the caller blocks on failure (see Guards); it must never try to repair the content and let it continue. For most of these the real control lives elsewhere anyway — parameterized queries / an ORM for SQL, a parser configured to disable external entities for XXE — so a validator that sanitizes the payload is security theater; detection is the only honest job it has.

  • Exception — sanitize-at-sink when the dangerous shape is also legitimate input. A few concerns can't be rejected because the thing that looks like an attack is also valid, user-authored content you must preserve — so detect-and-reject isn't an available move and output-encoding would destroy the meaning. For these, neutralizing in place is the correct control. It qualifies only when all three hold: (a) the content is legitimate input the user is entitled to send, not an attack wearing a disguise; (b) you use a vetted allowlist transform scoped to one specific sink — never a hand-rolled denylist; and (c) you apply it at that sink, not as a general "now it's clean" stamp. Safe for one sink is not safe for a different sink (SQL, a shell, an LLM prompt); never sanitize-then-forward across sinks.

    The one concern that qualifies today is HTML for display (WYSIWYG, markdown→HTML, rich comments): our HtmlSanitizer wraps nh3 (Rust ammonia), the server-side equivalent of OWASP's DOMPurify — an allowlist sanitizer over a real HTML5 parse tree, applied at the HTML render sink. A future validator earns this exception only by meeting the same three tests, not by analogy to HTML. - Mutation is for non-adversarial cleanup only. Reach for MutationGuard / mutate() when the issue is a quality or compliance concern on otherwise-trusted content — PII redaction, tone/casing/whitespace normalization, formatting fixes, stripping a banned-but-benign token. The content is not an attack; you are tidying it.

Why security must fail closed instead of mutating:

  • Sanitizing an attack and forwarding it gives a false sense of safety. One bypass you didn't model now flows downstream stamped "cleaned." Blocking fails closed; mutating fails open.
  • Mutating attacker-controlled input hands the attacker a second move — they craft input designed to survive your transform into a still-dangerous shape.
  • The safe response to an attack is to refuse it, not to negotiate with it.
Concern Example Category XSS / script injection (not for display) <script>…, onerror= in non-HTML content Detection only HTML for display user-authored rich text rendered as HTML Mutation OK (allowlist-sanitize at the render sink, vetted lib) Prompt / instruction injection "ignore previous instructions" Detection only SQL / command injection, XXE, SSRF ' OR 1=1, external-entity DTD Detection only (control lives at the sink) PII emails, phone numbers, national IDs Mutation OK (redact) Content quality tone, casing, whitespace, formatting Mutation OK (normalize) Banned benign tokens a disallowed brand name Mutation OK (strip)

Litmus test: if you can't honestly describe the job as "tidying trusted content," it is a security concern — build it detection-only. The sole exception is allowlist-sanitizing HTML at the render sink with a vetted library; if you're tempted to sanitize an attack payload for any other sink, you're negotiating with it — reject instead.

docs.title: The Validator Protocol
docs.text:
For use with Guard (detection only):

from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable
from aegis import GuardMetadata
from aegis.validators import ContentView, ValidationResult

@runtime_checkable
class Validator(Protocol):
    @property
    def name(self) -> str: ...

    async def validate(
        self,
        view: ContentView,
        metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
    ) -> ValidationResult: ...

Any class satisfying this protocol can be passed to Guard.use().

docs.title: Writing a Detection Validator
docs.text: The recommended approach is to subclass BaseValidator — it provides a default name (the class name) and makes the protocol requirement explicit via ABC. But a plain class works just as well.

docs.title: Using BaseValidator (recommended)
docs.text:
from aegis import BaseValidator, PassedResult, FailedResult

class ProfanityFilter(BaseValidator):
    """Blocks requests containing known profanity."""

    PROFANITY = {"badword1", "badword2"}

    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        value = view.render()
        found = [w for w in self.PROFANITY if w in value.lower()]
        if found:
            return FailedResult(
                error_message=f"Profanity detected: {found}",
                error_code="PROFANITY_DETECTED",
                details={"matches": found},
            )
        return PassedResult()

docs.title: Protocol-only (no subclassing)
docs.text:
from aegis import PassedResult, FailedResult

class ProfanityFilter:
    """Satisfies the Validator protocol without subclassing."""

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return "ProfanityFilter"

    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        value = view.render()
        if "badword" in value.lower():
            return FailedResult(
                error_message="Profanity detected",
                error_code="PROFANITY_DETECTED",
            )
        return PassedResult()

Both work identically in Guard.use().

docs.title: The MutationValidator Protocol
docs.text:
For use with MutationGuard (detect + fix). Like the detection Validator, it's view-based (validate(view)); it additionally implements mutate(view), which returns id-addressed edits the engine applies while guaranteeing part count and order are preserved.

from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable
from aegis import GuardMetadata
from aegis.validators import ContentView, FailedResult, ItemEdit, ValidationResult

@runtime_checkable
class MutationValidator(Protocol):
    @property
    def name(self) -> str: ...

    async def validate(
        self,
        view: ContentView,
        metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
    ) -> ValidationResult: ...

    async def mutate(
        self,
        view: ContentView,
        metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
        validation_failure: FailedResult | None = None,
    ) -> list[ItemEdit]: ...

mutate() is only called when validate() returns a FailedResult; it receives that failure as validation_failure.

docs.title: What a mutator sees and returns
docs.text:
• ContentView — the message's content items, in order. Iterate view.items (each is a ContentItem with a stable id, a type — a ContentType enum, ContentType.TEXT today — and its value), or call view.render() to get all the text joined with newlines for cross-part context.
  • ItemEdit(id, value) — a whole-item replacement addressed by id. Return one per item you want to change; items you don't address are left untouched. Returning edits for every item is equally valid — an edit that repeats an item's existing value is a no-op — so a partial list (only the ids you changed) and a full list produce identical output. Edits are keyed by id over the original items, so order doesn't matter and a repeated id takes its last value.

The engine rebuilds the view from your edits over the original items, so item count and order are preserved by construction — an item you don't address keeps its value. An edit whose id doesn't match an item raises MutationError. (Under an A2A agent, the view only ever exposes text items, and the guarded wrapper carries non-text parts such as images through untouched — see the A2A wrapper for how a validator plugs in.)

A mutation validator also works detect-only in Guard

Both protocols are view-based, so a MutationValidator is a superset of Validator: the same class can be registered with Guard for detection only (its validate runs; mutate is never called) or with MutationGuard to also fix. One class covers both.

docs.title: Writing a Mutation Validator
docs.text:
Detect on the view, then return one ItemEdit per part you want to rewrite:

from aegis import BaseMutationValidator, PassedResult, FailedResult, ItemEdit

class UppercaseNormalizer(BaseMutationValidator):
    """Detects ALL CAPS text parts and normalizes each to sentence case."""

    def _is_caps(self, text: str) -> bool:
        return text.isupper() and len(text) > 3

    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        if any(self._is_caps(p.value) for p in view.items):
            return FailedResult(error_message="Text is all uppercase", error_code="ALL_CAPS")
        return PassedResult()

    async def mutate(self, view, metadata=None, validation_failure=None):
        return [
            ItemEdit(p.id, p.value.capitalize())
            for p in view.items
            if self._is_caps(p.value)
        ]

Usage:

from aegis import ContentItem, ContentType, ContentView, MutationGuard

guard = MutationGuard("normalizer").use(UppercaseNormalizer())

# Single string in, single string out (convenience for the common one-item case):
result = await guard.validate("HELLO WORLD")
if result.was_mutated:
    print(result.output)   # "Hello world" — str in → output is a str

# Multiple parts: pass a ContentView, read the mutated view back.
view = ContentView(items=(
    ContentItem(id="p0", type=ContentType.TEXT, value="HELLO"),
    ContentItem(id="p1", type=ContentType.TEXT, value="world"),
))
result = await guard.validate(view)
if result.was_mutated:
    print(result.output.render())      # flattened text, parts joined by newline
    for item in result.output.items:   # same ids, count, and order as the input
        print(item.id, item.value)

output mirrors the input type: a str when you passed a str, otherwise a ContentView with the same items — same ids, count, and order — as the input. Read it with result.output.render() for the flattened text or result.output.items for per-part access. When a validator runs under an A2A agent, the guarded wrapper maps the transport's parts to and from this view for you, so a validator never touches transport types.

docs.title: Using cross-part context
docs.text:
Because mutate() receives the whole message, a mutator can make decisions that need surrounding parts — the reason the contract is view-based. Read view.render() for the joined text and still return whole-part edits:

class ToneRewriter(BaseMutationValidator):
    def __init__(self, llm):
        self.llm = llm

    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        return FailedResult(error_message="tone check", error_code="TONE")

    async def mutate(self, view, metadata=None, validation_failure=None):
        context = view.render()            # all parts, in order — cross-part context
        edits = []
        for p in view.items:
            rewritten = await self.llm.rewrite(p.value, context=context)
            if rewritten != p.value:
                edits.append(ItemEdit(p.id, rewritten))
        return edits

You own the model call, batching, and latency budget; the engine only guarantees the message shape. Whole-part rewrite means rewrite each part in place — you cannot merge two parts into one or split one into two (cardinality is fixed).

docs.title: Basic pattern
docs.text:
from aegis import Guard

async def test_profanity_filter_blocks_badwords():
    guard = Guard("test").use(ProfanityFilter())
    result = await guard.validate("This contains badword1")
    assert result.has_failures
    assert result.failures[0].error_code == "PROFANITY_DETECTED"

async def test_profanity_filter_passes_clean_text():
    guard = Guard("test").use(ProfanityFilter())
    result = await guard.validate("This is perfectly fine")
    assert not result.has_failures

docs.title: Mutation validators
docs.text:
Drive them through MutationGuard; assert on result.output — for a str input it is the mutated str directly, and for a ContentView input use result.output.render() for the flattened text or result.output.items for per-part access. Item count and order are guaranteed, so they are worth asserting too:

from aegis import ContentItem, ContentType, ContentView, MutationGuard

async def test_uppercase_normalizer_single_part():
    guard = MutationGuard("test").use(UppercaseNormalizer())
    result = await guard.validate("HELLO WORLD")
    assert result.was_mutated
    assert result.output == "Hello world"   # str in → output is a str

async def test_uppercase_normalizer_preserves_item_count_and_order():
    view = ContentView(items=(
        ContentItem(id="p0", type=ContentType.TEXT, value="HELLO"),
        ContentItem(id="p1", type=ContentType.TEXT, value="already fine"),
    ))
    guard = MutationGuard("test").use(UppercaseNormalizer())
    result = await guard.validate(view)
    assert result.was_mutated
    assert [i.id for i in result.output.items] == ["p0", "p1"]  # count + order preserved
    assert result.output.items[0].value == "Hello"             # caps item normalized
    assert result.output.items[1].value == "already fine"      # untouched, in place

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use specific error codes — prefer PROFANITY_DETECTED over VALIDATION_FAILED. Callers use codes programmatically.
  • Populate details — include enough context for callers to understand what failed and why.
  • Handle None metadata gracefully — metadata can be None. Both Validator and MutationValidator receive a ContentView (view.items may be empty but is never None); call view.render() for the flattened text. Check metadata before accessing.
  • Return edits only for parts you changed — in mutate(), emit a ItemEdit per part you actually rewrite; skipping unchanged parts keeps the diff minimal and the intent clear. Every ItemEdit.id must match a text part in the view, or the engine raises MutationError.
  • Keep validate() and mutate() independent — mutate() receives the FailedResult from validate() via validation_failure=; use that to know what to fix rather than re-running detection logic.
