docs.text: See Installation for setup instructions.

docs.title: Recommended Path — A2A Wrapper
docs.text:
If you're building an A2A agent with a standard AgentExecutor, the wrapper is the fastest path. Configure your guards once in InputGuardConfig / OutputGuardConfig objects, and the wrapper applies them transparently to every request — rejecting bad input, sanitizing output — without touching your execute() logic.

ContentFilter below is a built-in validator; PIIRedactor is a custom one you write against the contract. Aegis ships built-in validators (see Validators) and lets you add your own (see Custom Validators).

from aegis import Guard, MutationGuard, OnFailAction
from aegis.a2a import GuardedAgentExecutor, InputGuardConfig, OutputGuardConfig
from aegis.validators.detection import ContentFilter
from my_validators import PIIRedactor  # your own validators
from agent_config import BLOCKED_TOPICS

guarded = GuardedAgentExecutor(
    executor=MyExecutor(),
    input_config=InputGuardConfig(
        guard=(
            Guard("input")
            .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
        ),
        on_fail="I'm unable to help with that request.",
    ),
    output_config=OutputGuardConfig(
        mutation_guard=MutationGuard("output").use(PIIRedactor()),
    ),
)

Or use the @guarded decorator — same config objects, class-level syntax:

from aegis import Guard, MutationGuard, OnFailAction
from aegis.a2a import guarded, InputGuardConfig, OutputGuardConfig
from aegis.validators.detection import ContentFilter
from my_validators import PIIRedactor  # your own validators

@guarded(
    input_config=InputGuardConfig(
        guard=Guard("input").use(ContentFilter(...), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP),
        on_fail="I'm unable to help with that request.",
    ),
    output_config=OutputGuardConfig(
        mutation_guard=MutationGuard("output").use(PIIRedactor()),
    ),
)
class MyExecutor(AgentExecutor):
    async def execute(self, context, event_queue):
        query = context.get_user_input()  # mutated input if mutation_guard was set
        ...

See A2A Wrapper for the full reference — config objects, failure handling, pipeline ordering, and telemetry.

docs.title: Manual Integration — Guard and MutationGuard
docs.text: When you need full control — custom rejection messages per validator, streaming state machines, structured logging — use the primitives directly.

docs.title: Guard
docs.text:
Runs all validators concurrently and returns a GuardResult. Values are never modified.

from aegis import Guard, OnFailAction
from aegis.validators.detection import ContentFilter
from my_validators import PIIDetector  # your own validator
from agent_config import BLOCKED_TOPICS

input_guard = (
    Guard("input")
    .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
    .use(PIIDetector(), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
)

result = await input_guard.validate(value=user_message)
if result.has_failures:
    for failure in result.failures:
        print(f"{failure.validator_name}: {failure.error_message}")

See Guard for the full API reference.

docs.title: MutationGuard
docs.text:
Runs validators sequentially. When a validator fails, its mutate() is called and the corrected value is passed to the next validator.

from aegis import MutationGuard
from my_validators import PIIRedactor, ToneNormalizer  # your own validators

output_guard = (
    MutationGuard("output")
    .use(PIIRedactor())
    .use(ToneNormalizer())
)

result = await output_guard.validate(agent_response)
final = result.output if result.was_mutated else agent_response   # str in → output is a str

See MutationGuard for the full API reference.

docs.title: Failure Handling
docs.text:
The on_fail parameter on each .use() call controls what happens when that validator fails:

Action Behaviour OnFailAction.LOG Logs a warning (default) OnFailAction.EXCEPTION Raises ValidationError OnFailAction.NOOP Does nothing Custom callable Called with (result, validated_value, metadata) 
def notify_slack(result, validated_value, metadata):
    print(f"ALERT: {result.error_message}")

guard = Guard("alerts").use(PIIDetector(), on_fail=notify_slack)

docs.title: Writing a Custom Validator
docs.text:
Validators satisfy a structural protocol — any class with the right methods qualifies. BaseValidator is an optional convenience base class.

from aegis import BaseValidator, PassedResult, FailedResult

class ProfanityFilter(BaseValidator):
    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        value = view.render()
        if "badword" in value.lower():
            return FailedResult(
                error_message="Profanity detected",
                error_code="PROFANITY",
            )
        return PassedResult()

guard = Guard("content").use(ProfanityFilter())

For a complete guide including mutation validators, see Custom Validators.

docs.title: Guard
docs.text:
Guard is a pure validation engine. All registered validators run concurrently on each validate() call — no value is ever modified. Use it to decide whether to proceed with a request: accept or reject content as-is.

Aegis ships built-in detection validators (see Validators); you can also write your own by subclassing BaseValidator (or satisfying the Validator protocol). A tiny custom one:

from aegis import Guard, OnFailAction
from aegis.validators import BaseValidator, PassedResult, FailedResult

class MaxLength(BaseValidator):
    def __init__(self, limit: int) -> None:
        self.limit = limit
    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        value = view.render()
        if value and len(value) > self.limit:
            return FailedResult(error_message="too long", error_code="TOO_LONG")
        return PassedResult()

class BlockTopic(BaseValidator):
    def __init__(self, term: str) -> None:
        self.term = term
    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        value = view.render()
        if value and self.term in value.lower():
            return FailedResult(error_message="blocked topic", error_code="CONTENT_BLOCKED")
        return PassedResult()

input_guard = (
    Guard("input")
    .use(MaxLength(5000), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
    .use(BlockTopic("fraud"), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
)

See Custom Validators for the full guide.

docs.title: Creating a Guard
docs.text: guard = Guard("my-guard")  # name is used in telemetry spans and logs

docs.title: Opt-in text normalization
docs.text:
For homoglyph / variation-selector / NFKC bypass protection, construct the guard with normalize=True:

guard = Guard("input", normalize=True)

When normalize=True, the guard applies (NFKC fold → variation-selector strip → homoglyph→ASCII map) once to value and to the text of any text part in parts, then fans out the canonical form to every validator. Validators see the normalized text for matching; non-text parts pass through untouched.

The original value / parts arguments are never mutated and the normalized form does not escape via GuardResult — on pass, the caller forwards the untouched original to the agent.

text = "check ѕocials please"  # Cyrillic ѕ (U+0455)
guard = Guard("input", normalize=True).use(BlockTopic("socials"))
result = await guard.validate(value=text)
# result.has_failures == True   — homoglyph variant blocked
# text still == "check ѕocials please"  — caller's original is intact

Default is normalize=False. Leave it off for multilingual content where NFKC + homoglyph fold would corrupt legitimate non-ASCII text, and for guards built around raw-text validators (e.g. length or byte-size checks) where you want the unaltered byte counts.

normalize=True is a convenience alias for the engine profile. For finer control, pass a NormalizationConfig with per-strategy toggles instead of a bool — e.g. to NFKC-fold and case-fold without the non-Latin-corrupting homoglyph step:

from aegis import Guard, NormalizationConfig

guard = Guard("input", normalize=NormalizationConfig(unicode_form="NFKC", casefold=True))

Note: MutationGuard does not have a normalize flag — its mutation validators always operate on raw text. Pair a normalizing detection Guard upstream of a MutationGuard when you need both homoglyph defence and sanitization.

docs.title: Registering Validators
docs.text:
Use the fluent .use() API. Each call registers a validator and returns the guard for chaining.

guard = (
    Guard("input-guard")
    .use(ValidatorA(), on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION)
    .use(ValidatorB(), on_fail=OnFailAction.LOG)
    .use(ValidatorC())  # defaults to LOG
)

.use() validates the protocol at registration time — it will raise TypeError immediately if the object does not satisfy the Validator protocol.

docs.title: validate()
docs.text:
result = await guard.validate("Some user input text")  # a plain string

For A2A messages, build a ContentView with the adapter helper (the A2A wrapper does this for you):

from aegis.a2a._utils import build_view

result = await guard.validate(build_view(context.message.parts))

validate accepts a str or a ContentView; validators receive the view (call view.render() for the flattened text, or iterate view.items).

docs.title: GuardResult
docs.text:
validate() returns a GuardResult:

Field Type Description results list[ValidationResult] All results — one per registered validator has_failures bool True if any validator returned FailedResult failures list[FailedResult] Filtered list of only the failing results 
result = await guard.validate(value=user_message)

if result.has_failures:
    for failure in result.failures:
        print(f"[{failure.validator_name}] {failure.error_message}")
        print(f"  error_code: {failure.error_code}")
        print(f"  details:    {failure.details}")

docs.title: on_fail per Validator
docs.text:
Each .use() call accepts an on_fail parameter that controls what happens when that validator returns FailedResult. This fires inside validate() before the result is returned to the caller.

Action Behaviour OnFailAction.LOG Logs a warning with validator name and error message (default) OnFailAction.EXCEPTION Raises ValidationError immediately — validate() does not return OnFailAction.NOOP Does nothing — result is collected silently Custom callable Called with (result, validated_value, metadata) — side effects only 
# EXCEPTION — hard stop, raises ValidationError
guard.use(BlockTopic("secrets"), on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION)

# NOOP — collect failures, decide later from GuardResult
guard.use(BlockTopic("fraud"), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)

# Custom callable — log to your system, then continue
def send_alert(result, validated_value, metadata):
    logger.warning("Validator %s failed: %s", result.validator_name, result.error_message)

guard.use(MaxLength(5000), on_fail=send_alert)

Tip

Use OnFailAction.NOOP when you want all validators to run and collect all failures before deciding what to do. Use OnFailAction.EXCEPTION for an immediate hard stop.

docs.title: Concurrent Execution
docs.text:
All validators registered on a Guard run simultaneously via asyncio.gather(). This means:

  • No value chaining — every validator receives the same original input. A later validator cannot see an earlier validator's side effects.
  • All validators always run — there is no short-circuit on the first failure (unless on_fail=EXCEPTION raises).
  • Order of results matches registration order, regardless of which validator finishes first.
validate(value)
  │
  ├── ValidatorA.validate()  ──┐
  ├── ValidatorB.validate()  ──┤── asyncio.gather() ──► GuardResult
  └── ValidatorC.validate()  ──┘

If you need mutation or sequential execution, use MutationGuard instead.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
aegis requires a2a-sdk (>=0.3.20,<2) and works with both the 0.3.x and 1.x majors. A single install works against either — Aegis detects the installed SDK at import time. See the a2a-sdk v1 migration notes for the API differences between the two.

Aegis ships the engine (Guard, MutationGuard), a set of built-in validators (see Validators), and the validator contract (Validator / MutationValidator protocols, BaseValidator / BaseMutationValidator) so you can write your own too (see Custom Validators).

Until the first release, install from the repository (Method 3) or from source (Method 4). A PyPI package will be the recommended install from the first release onward (Method 1).

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
Extra Pulls in Required for telemetry opentelemetry-sdk Exporting OpenTelemetry traces (the core only depends on the OTEL API, which is a no-op without an SDK)

There are four ways to consume aegis, depending on your context:

# Method When to use 1 PyPI Standard install 2 Vendored wheel Air-gapped environments or no network access at install time 3 Git URL When you need the latest unreleased changes 4 From source Contributors / active development

docs.title: Method 1 — PyPI (recommended)
docs.text:
Available from the first release. Until then, use Method 3 or 4. The PyPI distribution name is published with the first release; the <PYPI_PACKAGE_NAME> placeholder below marks where it goes.

pip install <PYPI_PACKAGE_NAME>

Pin it in requirements.txt:

<PYPI_PACKAGE_NAME>==1.0.0
requests==2.31.0
# ... other packages

pip install -r requirements.txt

If your project uses uv:

uv add <PYPI_PACKAGE_NAME>

In a Dockerfile, install from the committed requirements.txt — no credentials needed:

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Method 2 — Vendored wheel
docs.text:
Use this for air-gapped environments or anywhere without network access at install time. Committing the .whl into your repository means nothing is fetched at install time, in any environment.

Step 1 — Download the wheel from a GitHub Release:

gh release download v1.0.0 \
  --pattern '*.whl' \
  --repo SAP/project-aegis \
  --dir vendor/wheels/

Or copy the .whl file manually from the release assets.

Note: You can replace v1.0.0 with --latest to always download the most recent release. However, since the .whl filename embeds the version number, you will still need to update the filename reference in vendor/wheels/ and requirements.txt after each upgrade.

Step 2 — Add it to your repo layout:

your-app/
  vendor/
    wheels/
      <pypi_package_name>-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
  requirements.txt
  Dockerfile

Step 3 — Reference it in requirements.txt:

./vendor/wheels/<pypi_package_name>-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl

Step 4 — Install locally or in Docker:

# Local development
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Docker build
COPY requirements.txt .
COPY vendor/wheels/ ./vendor/wheels/

RUN pip install --no-cache -r requirements.txt

The same requirements.txt works in both contexts — no token injection needed anywhere.

docs.title: Method 3 — Git URL
docs.text:
Use this when you need changes that haven't been released yet:

pip install git+https://github.com/SAP/project-aegis.git

docs.title: Method 4 — From source (contributors)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/SAP/project-aegis.git
cd project-aegis
pip install -e ".[dev]"

docs.title: Updating to a new version
docs.text:
pip install --upgrade <PYPI_PACKAGE_NAME>

If using the vendored wheel approach: download the new .whl from the GitHub Release, replace the old one in vendor/wheels/, update the path in requirements.txt if the version changed, and commit both together.

docs.title: Releasing a new version (maintainers only)
docs.text:
Releases publish to PyPI via OIDC trusted publishing. The automated release workflow is configured once the project is public; once in place, it runs on every published GitHub Release.

Step 1 — Bump the version in pyproject.toml:

[project]
version = "1.0.0"

Step 2 — Tag and publish a GitHub Release:

The release tag must be v<version> (e.g. v1.0.0) — the release workflow validates that the tag matches the package version in pyproject.toml, then triggers uv build and the upload to PyPI; no local credentials are involved.

docs.title: MutationGuard
docs.text:
MutationGuard is a sequential mutation pipeline. Validators run in registration order — when one returns FailedResult, its mutate() is called; the resulting edits are applied and the rebuilt message is passed to the next validator. Use it to clean up content before passing it on: PII redaction, tone correction, normalization.

Aegis ships the HtmlSanitizer mutation validator (see Validators); you can also write your own by subclassing BaseMutationValidator with a validate() (detect) and mutate() (fix). Mutators are view-based: they see the message as a ContentView and return id-addressed ItemEdits. A tiny custom one that redacts emails:

import re
from aegis import MutationGuard
from aegis.validators import BaseMutationValidator, PassedResult, FailedResult, ItemEdit

EMAIL = re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+")

class EmailRedactor(BaseMutationValidator):
    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        if any(EMAIL.search(p.value) for p in view.items):
            return FailedResult(error_message="email present", error_code="PII_DETECTED")
        return PassedResult()

    async def mutate(self, view, metadata=None, validation_failure=None):
        return [
            ItemEdit(p.id, EMAIL.sub("<EMAIL>", p.value))
            for p in view.items if EMAIL.search(p.value)
        ]

output_guard = MutationGuard("output").use(EmailRedactor())

See Custom Validators for the full guide.

docs.title: Guard vs MutationGuard
docs.text: Guard MutationGuard Execution Concurrent Sequential Mutation Never When validator returns FailedResult Return type GuardResult MutationGuardResult on_fail per validator Yes No — always runs mutate() on failure Typical use Input validation, compliance, scope checking Output sanitization, PII redaction, tone correction

docs.title: Creating a MutationGuard
docs.text:
guard = MutationGuard("my-guard")  # name used in telemetry spans and logs

Text normalization is intentionally absent. MutationGuard operates on raw text — there is no normalize flag. Mutation validators match against whatever text the caller hands them and emit byte-equivalent output for the matched spans only.

If you need homoglyph / variation-selector / NFKC bypass protection on the mutation path, pair a normalizing detection Guard upstream that blocks the request before it reaches the mutation pipeline:

# Detect-and-block first; on pass, mutate the (untouched) original.
input_guard = Guard("input", normalize=True).use(
    BlockSocials(),
    on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION,
)
sanitizer = MutationGuard("sanitize").use(EmailRedactor())

await input_guard.validate(value=user_text)
result = await sanitizer.validate(value=user_text)

docs.title: Registering Validators
docs.text:
Use the fluent .use() API. Validators run in registration order.

guard = (
    MutationGuard("output-sanitizer")
    .use(EmailRedactor())    # runs first
    .use(ToneNormalizer())   # sees the output of EmailRedactor
)

.use() validates the protocol at registration time — it will raise TypeError immediately if the object does not satisfy the MutationValidator protocol (requires both validate() and mutate() methods).

docs.title: validate()
docs.text:
result = await guard.validate(value="Some agent response text")

For A2A parts, build a ContentView with the adapter helper (the A2A wrapper does this for you):

from aegis.a2a._utils import build_view

result = await guard.validate(build_view(artifact.parts))

docs.title: MutationGuardResult
docs.text:
validate() returns a MutationGuardResult:

Field Type Description was_mutated bool True if any validator changed the content output str \| ContentView \| None Final content, mirroring the input type: a str when you called validate with a str, otherwise a ContentView (same item count and order as the input). For the view case, call .render() for the flattened text results list[ValidationResult] All validation results (pass and fail) 
result = await guard.validate(agent_response)   # str in → str out

if result.was_mutated:
    final = result.output                  # already the mutated string (str in → str out)
else:
    final = agent_response                 # original unchanged

For A2A parts, the adapter helpers in aegis.a2a._utils convert to and from the view: build_view projects text parts into a ContentView (so a mutator sees the whole message via view.render()), and apply_view writes the mutated output back over the original parts — so [text, image, text] stays [text', image, text'], with non-text parts (DataPart, FilePart) passed through untouched in place. Item count and order are preserved.

from aegis.a2a._utils import apply_view, build_view

result = await guard.validate(build_view(artifact.parts))   # view in → output is a ContentView
if result.was_mutated:
    artifact = artifact.model_copy(update={"parts": apply_view(artifact.parts, result.output)})

The A2A executor / event-queue wrappers do this for you on the input and output stages. A mutator sees all parts together, so context-sensitive mutation (e.g. tone rewriting that depends on neighbouring parts) works.

docs.title: Sequential Execution
docs.text:
Validators run in the order they were registered. Each validator sees a fresh ContentView of the current parts — so a later validator sees the earlier one's edits:

build_view(parts)
  │
  ├── ValidatorA.validate(view)
  │       ├── PassedResult → no edits, parts unchanged
  │       └── FailedResult → ValidatorA.mutate(view) → edits → rebuild → parts_a
  │
  └── ValidatorB.validate(view of parts_a)   ← sees A's output
          ├── PassedResult → no edits
          └── FailedResult → ValidatorB.mutate(view) → edits → rebuild → parts_b (final)
  • A validator's mutate() is only called when its own validate() returns FailedResult.
  • Validators that return PassedResult apply no edits; the message is unchanged for that step.
  • output (a ContentView; call .render() for the single-text case) reflects the message after all mutations.

docs.title: Detect-only vs detect-and-fix
docs.text: Both Validator and MutationValidator are view-based (validate(view)), so a MutationValidator is a superset of Validator: the same class can be registered with Guard for detect-only use (its validate runs; mutate is never called) or with MutationGuard to also fix. See Custom Validators.

docs.title: AgentExecutor Integration
docs.text:
How to wire aegis into a standard A2A AgentExecutor. Two approaches are available:

Approach When to use GuardedAgentExecutor Standard input/output guardrails with minimal boilerplate Manual integration Full control over rejection logic, state machine, logging

docs.title: GuardedAgentExecutor Wrapper
docs.text:
The simplest path — wrap your executor with GuardedAgentExecutor and pass config objects for input and output. The wrapper handles guard execution, rejection, and output mutation transparently.

ContentFilter below is a built-in validator; MaxLength and PIIRedactor are custom ones you write against the contract. Aegis ships built-in validators (see Validators) and lets you add your own (see Custom Validators).

from aegis import Guard, MutationGuard, OnFailAction
from aegis.a2a import GuardedAgentExecutor, InputGuardConfig, OutputGuardConfig
from aegis.validators.detection import ContentFilter
from my_validators import MaxLength, PIIRedactor
from agent_config import BLOCKED_TOPICS

guarded_executor = GuardedAgentExecutor(
    executor=MyAgentExecutor(),
    input_config=InputGuardConfig(
        guard=(
            Guard("input")
            .use(MaxLength(5000), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
            .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
        ),
        on_fail="I'm unable to help with that request.",
    ),
    output_config=OutputGuardConfig(
        mutation_guard=MutationGuard("output").use(PIIRedactor()),
    ),
)

Or use the @guarded decorator:

from aegis.a2a import guarded, InputGuardConfig, OutputGuardConfig

@guarded(
    input_config=InputGuardConfig(
        guard=(
            Guard("input")
            .use(MaxLength(5000), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
            .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
        ),
        on_fail="I'm unable to help with that request.",
    ),
    output_config=OutputGuardConfig(
        mutation_guard=MutationGuard("output").use(PIIRedactor()),
    ),
)
class MyAgentExecutor(AgentExecutor):
    async def execute(self, context: RequestContext, event_queue: EventQueue) -> None:
        ...

docs.title: Reversing pipeline order
docs.text:
By default the input pipeline runs Guard → MutationGuard. Set mutation_first=True to sanitize input before checking it — useful when you want guards to check the cleaned version:

InputGuardConfig(
    guard=Guard("input").use(MaxLength(5000)).use(ContentFilter(...)),
    mutation_guard=MutationGuard("sanitize").use(PIIRedactor()),
    mutation_first=True,  # redact PII first, then check the clean input
    on_fail="I'm unable to help with that request.",
)

See Guardrail Lifecycle for how the default pipeline maps to the full A2A request cycle. See A2A Wrapper for full reference on config objects, failure handling, pipeline ordering, and telemetry.

docs.title: Manual Integration
docs.text:
Use this when you need full control — custom rejection messages per validator, structured logging, or non-standard task state handling.

This example targets the a2a-sdk 1.x API (the default install). On 0.3.x the a2a APIs differ — from a2a.utils import ..., Part(root=TextPart(text=...)), TaskState.rejected, update_status(..., final=True). See the migration notes for the mapping.

import logging
from a2a.server.agent_execution import AgentExecutor, RequestContext
from a2a.server.events import EventQueue
from a2a.server.tasks import TaskUpdater
from a2a.types import TaskState, Part
from a2a.helpers import new_task_from_user_message, new_text_message
from a2a.server.errors import ServerError, InternalError

from aegis import Guard, MutationGuard, OnFailAction
from aegis.validators.detection import ContentFilter
from my_validators import MaxLength, PIIRedactor  # your own validators
from agent_config import BLOCKED_TOPICS

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class MyAgentExecutor(AgentExecutor):
    def __init__(self):
        self.agent = MyAgent()
        self.guard = (
            Guard("input")
            .use(MaxLength(5000), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
            .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
        )
        self.mutate_guard = MutationGuard("output").use(PIIRedactor())

    async def execute(self, context: RequestContext, event_queue: EventQueue) -> None:
        query = context.get_user_input()
        task = context.current_task

        if not task:
            task = new_task_from_user_message(context.message)
            await event_queue.enqueue_event(task)

        updater = TaskUpdater(event_queue, task.id, task.context_id)

        # ── Input guard ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        results = await self.guard.validate(query)

        for failed_result in results.failures:
            logger.warning(
                "Input failed sensitivity check",
                extra={
                    "task_id": task.id,
                    "context_id": task.context_id,
                    "error_code": failed_result.error_code,
                    "error_message": failed_result.error_message,
                }
            )
            await updater.reject(
                new_text_message(failed_result.error_message, context_id=task.context_id, task_id=task.id)
            )
            return
        # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        try:
            async for item in self.agent.stream(
                query=query,
                context_id=task.context_id,
            ):
                is_task_complete = item["is_task_complete"]
                require_user_input = item["require_user_input"]
                content = item.get("content", "")
                metadata = item.get("metadata", {})

                if not is_task_complete and not require_user_input:
                    await updater.update_status(
                        TaskState.TASK_STATE_WORKING,
                        new_text_message(content, context_id=task.context_id, task_id=task.id),
                    )

                elif require_user_input:
                    await updater.requires_input(
                        new_text_message(content, context_id=task.context_id, task_id=task.id)
                    )
                    break

                else:
                    # ── Output mutation guard ──────────────────────────────────
                    mutation_result = await self.mutate_guard.validate(content)
                    output_value = mutation_result.output if mutation_result.was_mutated else content

                    logger.info(
                        "Output after mutation guard",
                        extra={
                            "task_id": task.id,
                            "context_id": task.context_id,
                            "was_mutated": mutation_result.was_mutated,
                            "output_length": len(output_value) if output_value else 0,
                        },
                    )
                    # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

                    parts = [Part(text=output_value)]

                    structured_data = item.get("structured_data")
                    if structured_data:
                        metadata["structured_data"] = structured_data

                    await updater.add_artifact(parts, name="result", metadata=metadata)
                    await updater.complete()
                    break

        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(
                "Error while executing agent",
                extra={"task_id": task.id, "error": str(e)},
                exc_info=True,
            )
            raise ServerError(error=InternalError()) from e

docs.title: Input Guard — Before Streaming
docs.text:
• OnFailAction.NOOP lets all validators run and collects all failures before deciding
  • updater.reject(...) closes the task cleanly with a terminal rejected status
  • return after the first failure — no reason to send multiple rejection messages

docs.title: Stream State Machine
docs.text: is_task_complete require_user_input A2A State Action False False working Status update, keep streaming False True input_required Status update, final=True, break True False completed Run output guard, add artifact, complete

docs.title: Output Mutation Guard — On Completion
docs.text:
• Only runs on the completed branch — not on working updates or input_required
  • guarded by mutation_result.was_mutated — we use mutation_result.output (a str, since content is a str) when it changed, else fall back to content

docs.title: Guard Placement
docs.text:
RequestContext
    │
    ▼
Task setup (new_task / existing task)
    │
    ▼
Input guard ──── fails ──▶ reject() + return
    │
    passes
    ▼
agent.stream()
    ├── working        ──▶ TaskState.TASK_STATE_WORKING
    ├── input_required ──▶ requires_input() + break
    └── completed      ──▶ Output mutation guard ──▶ add_artifact + complete

docs.title: agent.stream() Integration
docs.text:
How to wire aegis inside the agent's stream() method — the layer that runs the underlying graph and yields response items back to the executor.

Guards here run before the graph is invoked, keeping the graph itself free of guardrail logic. The executor (the A2A layer above) handles converting guard results into A2A protocol responses — see AgentExecutor Integration.

The examples below use Guard for input (detect and reject). You can also use a MutationGuard for input — for example, redacting PII from the query before it reaches the graph. See Standalone Usage — Guard Combinations.

docs.title: Guard Initialization
docs.text:
Build the guard once in __init__, not per-request.

ContentFilter is a built-in validator and MaxLength is a custom one you write against the contract. Aegis ships built-in validators (see Validators) and lets you add your own (see Custom Validators).

from aegis import Guard, OnFailAction
from aegis.validators.detection import ContentFilter
from my_validators import MaxLength  # your own validator
from agent_config import BLOCKED_TOPICS


class MyAgent:
    def __init__(self):
        self.input_guard = (
            Guard("my-agent-input")
            .use(MaxLength(5000), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
            .use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=BLOCKED_TOPICS), on_fail=OnFailAction.NOOP)
        )

OnFailAction.NOOP keeps all validators running and returns failures for the caller to inspect — no exceptions, no implicit logging.

docs.title: Running the Guard and Yielding a Rejection
docs.text:
Run the guard at the top of stream(). On failure, yield a completed response item and return — the graph is never invoked.

async def stream(self, query: str, context_id: str):
    guard_result = await self.input_guard.validate(value=query)

    if guard_result.has_failures:
        failure = guard_result.failures[0]

        # Build message based on which validator fired
        if failure.error_code == "CONTENT_BLOCKED":
            message = "I'm unable to assist with that request."
        else:
            message = "That request can't be processed. Please rephrase and try again."

        yield {
            "is_task_complete": True,
            "require_user_input": False,
            "content": message,
            "metadata": {"guardrail": failure.details},
        }
        return  # Graph never runs

    # Guard passed — invoke graph
    result = await self.graph.ainvoke(build_state(query, context_id))
    yield {
        "is_task_complete": True,
        "require_user_input": False,
        "content": result["final_response"],
    }

Including failure.details in the yielded item's metadata lets the executor (and the A2A caller) see structured context — e.g. matched_topic from ContentFilter.

docs.title: Full stream() Pattern
docs.text:
async def stream(self, query: str, context_id: str):
    # 1. Input guard
    guard_result = await self.input_guard.validate(value=query)

    if guard_result.has_failures:
        failure = guard_result.failures[0]
        yield {
            "is_task_complete": True,
            "require_user_input": False,
            "content": self._rejection_message(failure),
            "metadata": {"guardrail": failure.details},
        }
        return

    # 2. Build state
    input_state = {
        "messages": [HumanMessage(content=query)],
        "thread_id": context_id,
    }

    # 3. Run graph
    yield {
        "is_task_complete": False,
        "require_user_input": False,
        "content": "Analyzing your request...",
    }

    result = await self.graph.ainvoke(
        input_state,
        config={"configurable": {"thread_id": context_id}},
    )

    # 4. Output mutation guard — redact PII and normalize tone before returning
    raw_response = result["final_response"]
    mutation_result = await self.output_guard.validate(raw_response)
    final_response = mutation_result.output if mutation_result.was_mutated else raw_response

    yield {
        "is_task_complete": True,
        "require_user_input": False,
        "content": final_response,
        "metadata": result.get("metadata", {}),
    }

def _rejection_message(self, failure) -> str:
    if failure.error_code == "CONTENT_BLOCKED":
        return "I'm unable to assist with that request."
    return "That request can't be processed. Please rephrase and try again."

output_guard is a MutationGuard initialised in __init__ alongside the input guard:

from aegis import MutationGuard
from my_validators import PIIRedactor  # your own MutationValidator

class MyAgent:
    def __init__(self):
        self.output_guard = MutationGuard("my-agent-output").use(PIIRedactor())

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Patterns for monitoring guard activity without necessarily blocking requests.

OpenTelemetry / auto-instrumentation

Full observability guidance — including auto-instrumentation for trace correlation and metrics export — is pending. More details will be added once that integration is validated.

docs.title: Soft Guardrails — Observe Without Blocking
docs.text:
During rollout or for non-critical checks, observe violations without interrupting the flow. Useful for building a violation baseline before deciding to enforce.

# Option A: LOG action — emits a warning, never raises
# PIIDetector here is a custom validator you write; Aegis also ships built-in ones
guard = Guard("soft").use(PIIDetector(), on_fail=OnFailAction.LOG)

result = await guard.validate(value=user_message)
# Always continues — failures are logged but execution proceeds
if result.has_failures:
    for f in result.failures:
        metrics.increment("pii_detected", tags={"validator": f.validator_name})

# Option B: custom callable for structured audit logging
async def record_violation(result, validated_value, metadata):
    logger.warning(
        "Guard violation",
        extra={
            "error_code": result.error_code,
            "error_message": result.error_message,
            "details": result.details,
        },
    )
    await audit_log.record(result)
    # Do NOT raise here — observe-only
    # Add a raise to promote this to a hard block when ready to enforce

guard = Guard("audit").use(
    ContentFilter(blocked_topics=["fraud"]),
    on_fail=record_violation,
)

The custom callable can be promoted to a hard block at any point by adding a raise — no other code changes needed.

docs.title: Log Output Mutations
docs.text:
out.was_mutated tells you whether any validator changed the content, and out.output carries the final result — a str when you passed a str, otherwise a ContentView (call out.output.render() for the text). Per-validator outcomes (pass and fail) are in out.results; the failures that triggered a fix are out.failures.

out = await output_guard.validate(raw_response)   # str in → out.output is a str

if out.was_mutated:
    logger.info(
        "Output sanitized",
        extra={
            "triggered_by": [f.validator_name for f in out.failures],
            "output": out.output,
        },
    )
    metrics.increment("output_mutations")

docs.title: Inspect All Results, Not Just Failures
docs.text:
guard_result.results contains every validator's outcome — passes included. Useful for confirming that a validator ran even when it didn't fire.

guard_result = await guard.validate(value=query)

for r in guard_result.results:
    logger.debug(
        "Validator result",
        extra={
            "validator": r.validator_name,
            "passed": not isinstance(r, FailedResult),
        },
    )

docs.title: Standalone Usage
docs.text:
How to use aegis outside of an A2A executor — in scripts, tests, batch jobs, or any context where you call validate() directly and interpret the result yourself.

Aegis ships built-in validators, but the examples below define small custom ones inline to show the contract. See Custom Validators for the full guide; a minimal set:

from aegis.validators import (
    BaseValidator, BaseMutationValidator, PassedResult, FailedResult, ItemEdit,
)

class MaxLength(BaseValidator):
    def __init__(self, limit: int) -> None:
        self.limit = limit
    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        value = view.render()
        if value and len(value) > self.limit:
            return FailedResult(error_message="too long", error_code="TOO_LONG")
        return PassedResult()

class BlockTopic(BaseValidator):
    def __init__(self, term: str) -> None:
        self.term = term
    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        value = view.render()
        if value and self.term in value.lower():
            return FailedResult(error_message="blocked topic", error_code="CONTENT_BLOCKED")
        return PassedResult()

class EmailRedactor(BaseMutationValidator):
    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        if any("@" in p.value for p in view.items):
            return FailedResult(error_message="email present", error_code="PII_DETECTED")
        return PassedResult()
    async def mutate(self, view, metadata=None, validation_failure=None):
        return [ItemEdit(p.id, "[EMAIL_REDACTED]") for p in view.items if "@" in p.value]

docs.title: Guard — Interpreting GuardResult
docs.text:
guard.validate() always returns a GuardResult. It never raises unless a validator was registered with on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION.

from aegis import Guard, OnFailAction

guard = (
    Guard("my-guard")
    .use(MaxLength(5000))
    .use(EmailRedactor())  # a MutationValidator used detect-only
    .use(BlockTopic("fraud"))
)

result = await guard.validate(value="Some input text")

GuardResult fields:

Field Type Description has_failures bool True if any validator returned a FailedResult failures list[FailedResult] All failures only results list[ValidationResult] Every validator's result — passes and failures

docs.title: Check for failures
docs.text:
if result.has_failures:
    for failure in result.failures:
        print(f"{failure.validator_name}: [{failure.error_code}] {failure.error_message}")
        print(f"  details: {failure.details}")
else:
    print("All checks passed")

docs.title: Inspect all results (passes included)
docs.text:
for r in result.results:
    status = "FAIL" if isinstance(r, FailedResult) else "PASS"
    print(f"[{status}] {r.validator_name}")

docs.title: Raise on first failure
docs.text:
Register with on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION to raise immediately instead of collecting:

from aegis import ValidationError

guard = Guard("strict").use(EmailRedactor(), on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION)

try:
    await guard.validate(value=user_input)
except ValidationError as e:
    print(f"Blocked: [{e.result.error_code}] {e.result.error_message}")
    print(f"Details: {e.result.details}")

ValidationError carries the FailedResult as .result — same fields as above.

docs.title: MutationGuard — Interpreting MutationGuardResult
docs.text:
mutation_guard.validate() returns a MutationGuardResult. The output field holds the final ContentView; call .render() for the text. Use was_mutated to see if anything changed.

from aegis import MutationGuard

guard = MutationGuard("sanitizer").use(EmailRedactor())

result = await guard.validate(value="Hey!! Contact me at user@example.com 😊")

MutationGuardResult fields:

Field Type Description was_mutated bool True if any validator changed the content output str \| ContentView \| None Final content, mirroring the input type — a str when you passed a str, otherwise a ContentView (same item count and order; .render() for text) results list[ValidationResult] Full pass/fail record for all validators

docs.title: Apply the mutated output
docs.text:
# str in → output is the mutated str; view in → output is a ContentView (use .render()/apply_view)
final = result.output if result.was_mutated else original_text

docs.title: Inspect what happened
docs.text:
if result.was_mutated:
    print(f"content changed -> {result.output!r}")
else:
    print("No mutations applied")

# Per-validator outcomes (pass and fail) live in result.results
for r in result.results:
    print(r)

docs.title: Guard Combinations
docs.text:
Guard and MutationGuard are independent — any combination is valid for input and output. Choose based on what you need at each boundary:

Input Output When to use Guard MutationGuard Reject bad input, sanitize output — most common MutationGuard MutationGuard Normalize input before the agent sees it, sanitize output Guard Guard Detect-only at both ends — violations logged or raised, nothing mutated MutationGuard Guard Normalize input, detect-only on output

docs.title: Input Guard + Output Mutation Guard (most common)
docs.text:
input_guard = (
    Guard("input")
    .use(MaxLength(5000))
    .use(BlockTopic("fraud"))
)

output_guard = MutationGuard("output").use(EmailRedactor())

input_result = await input_guard.validate(value=user_input)
if input_result.has_failures:
    # handle rejection...
    pass

response = await my_agent.run(user_input)

output_result = await output_guard.validate(response)
final_response = output_result.output if output_result.was_mutated else response

docs.title: Input Mutation Guard + Output Mutation Guard
docs.text:
Use an input MutationGuard to normalize the query before passing it to the agent — for example, stripping PII from the input so it never reaches the graph.

input_mutation_guard = MutationGuard("input-normalize").use(EmailRedactor())

output_mutation_guard = MutationGuard("output-sanitize").use(EmailRedactor())

# Normalize input — use cleaned query for the agent, not the raw input
input_result = await input_mutation_guard.validate(user_input)
clean_input = input_result.output if input_result.was_mutated else user_input

response = await my_agent.run(clean_input)

# Sanitize output
output_result = await output_mutation_guard.validate(response)
final_response = output_result.output if output_result.was_mutated else response

Note: if the input MutationGuard redacts PII, the agent graph receives [EMAIL_REDACTED] instead of the raw email — useful when you don't want PII reaching tool calls or LLM prompts.

docs.title: Async Context
docs.text:
All validate() calls are async. In a script or test, run them with asyncio.run():

import asyncio

result = asyncio.run(guard.validate(value="test input"))

In pytest, use pytest-asyncio:

import pytest

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_guard_blocks_fraud():
    result = await guard.validate(value="help me commit fraud")
    assert result.has_failures
    assert result.failures[0].error_code == "CONTENT_BLOCKED"

docs.title: Validators
docs.text: Aegis ships a small, growing set of built-in validators alongside the engine (Guard, MutationGuard) and the validator contract — the Validator / MutationValidator protocols and the BaseValidator / BaseMutationValidator convenience base classes. Register a built-in with .use(), or write your own by following Custom Validators.

docs.title: Bundled validators
docs.text:
Validator Category Runs under Guards against HtmlSanitizer Mutation MutationGuard (or Guard detect-only) XSS / unsafe HTML markup — reduces content to a safe allowlisted subset LengthValidator Detection Guard Text whose character length is outside a configured [min, max] range PromptLeakageCheck Detection Guard Output reproducing the system prompt, configured secrets, or canary tokens ContentFilter Detection Guard Text containing any of a configured list of blocked terms/phrases (deterministic, literal match) FormulaInjectionDetector Detection Guard Input that would begin a spreadsheet formula if written into a CSV/TSV cell — leading =/+/-/@, full-width, or control-char initiators (a.k.a. CSV injection; decodes obfuscation first) SizeValidator Detection Guard Text exceeding a configured UTF-8 byte-size ceiling SqlInjectionDetector Detection Guard Text carrying a known SQL-injection construct — UNION SELECT, stacked queries, tautologies, comments, time-based probes (decodes obfuscation first) XssDetector Detection Guard Text carrying a known cross-site-scripting (XSS) vector — HTML tags, script URIs, DOM sinks (decodes obfuscation first) XxeDetector Detection Guard Text carrying an XXE construct — external entities, external/inline DTDs, entity declarations, XInclude (decodes obfuscation first; masks inert comment/CDATA/PI regions)

More built-ins are planned. To write one, see the Authoring Guide.

Opt-in Unicode normalization on Guard

To defeat bypasses where an attacker disguises a banned token with visually identical but bytewise different characters (e.g. Cyrillic ѕ U+0455 instead of ASCII s), construct your detection guard with Guard("input", normalize=True). The guard applies NFKC + variation-selector strip + homoglyph→ASCII fold once before fanning out to validators; the caller's original text is forwarded to the agent on pass.

MutationGuard does not normalize text. Pair a normalizing detection Guard upstream when you need homoglyph protection on the mutation path. See Architecture.

docs.title: The Contract
docs.text:
Everything you need to build a validator is importable from aegis or aegis.validators:

Symbol Purpose Validator Protocol for detection validators (used with Guard) MutationValidator Protocol for detect-and-fix validators (used with MutationGuard) BaseValidator Optional base class for detection validators BaseMutationValidator Optional base class for mutation validators PassedResult / FailedResult Return values from validate() ContentView / ContentItem The content a validator sees (validate(view)) ItemEdit Id-addressed whole-part edit returned from mutate()

One class can do both

Both protocols are view-based (validate(view)), so a MutationValidator is a superset of Validator: the same class runs under Guard for detection only (validate runs; mutate is not called) or under MutationGuard to also fix.

See Custom Validators — MutationValidator Protocol for a full explanation.

docs.title: Writing Your Own
docs.text: Any class satisfying the Validator or MutationValidator protocol works as a validator. Start with the Custom Validators contract, then follow the Authoring Guide for where code/tests/docs live and the end-to-end workflow.

docs.title: Authoring Guide
docs.text:
This guide is the end-to-end walkthrough for adding a validator to Aegis: where the code, tests, and docs live, how a validator is registered, and the workflow that takes it from an idea to a shippable component.

It builds on Custom Validators, which is the contract reference — the protocols, result types, and the detect-vs-mutate rule. Read that first to learn what a validator must implement; read this to learn where it goes and how to ship it.

Prerequisites

Set up your environment first — see the project's CONTRIBUTING.md for pip install -e ".[dev]", the pre-commit hooks, and the commit-message convention.

docs.title: Workflow at a glance
docs.text:
Every new validator goes through the same four steps. They lean on a few durable engineering practices — design before you code, defend against bad input, hide internals:

  1. Research, then spec it — research is mandatory and comes first. Study the domain and any standard that governs it before you define the contract: a PII redactor, for example, takes its definition of "personal data" and its redaction rules from the applicable regulation (GDPR and its equivalents), not from intuition. Requirements you assume instead of research are the ones that leak in production.

Turn that research into an explicit, written spec before any code — what the validator validates, its input/output contract, its edge cases, and what it deliberately leaves out of scope. Defining the intent before the implementation (construct-by-intent) is the cheapest place to be wrong. Keep the spec a living description — the module/class docstring is a good home — and update it as the implementation evolves. 2. Implement to the spec — write the validator against the contract (see Custom Validators), then harden it. Treat every input as hostile and barricade it: malformed, empty, and adversarial input are the normal case for a validator, not the exception (defensive programming). Keep it to one concern — one validator checks one thing — and its public surface minimal: one class, helpers _-private (information hiding). Conform the signatures and return types exactly, and match the folder/file layout below. 3. Test it thoroughly — cover the happy path, boundaries, error paths, and malformed input. Boundary and error cases are where defects concentrate, and a validator is a security surface — miss nothing. 4. Peer review — a second pair of eyes before it merges. Include the spec, code, tests, and docs in the same PR.

The rest of this page details the layout and conventions each step relies on.

docs.title: The contract, in brief
docs.text:
Your validator is a class that implements the methods below — either by subclassing BaseValidator / BaseMutationValidator, or by matching the protocol directly. The signatures are fixed: implement them exactly as shown; don't rename parameters or change the return types. This section is a quick recap only — Custom Validators is the authoritative contract reference, with the full explanation and worked examples.

# Every validator implements validate() — it receives a ContentView (under Guard or MutationGuard):
async def validate(self, view: ContentView, metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None) -> ValidationResult

# Mutation validators additionally implement mutate() — MutationGuard calls it after a
# FailedResult to fix, returning id-addressed edits:
async def mutate(
    self,
    view: ContentView,
    metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
    validation_failure: FailedResult | None = None,
) -> list[ItemEdit]
  • validate() (and mutate()) receive a ContentView — call view.render() for the flattened text, or iterate view.items for per-item / cross-item context. metadata is a GuardMetadata dataclass or None (check before accessing).
  • validate() returns PassedResult or FailedResult; put extra context in the details mapping. Every FailedResult gets a stable, specific error_code.
  • mutate() returns list[ItemEdit] — one id-addressed whole-part replacement per part it changes; the engine rebuilds over the original parts, preserving count and order.

docs.title: Where code lives
docs.text:
Validators live under src/aegis/validators/, split by what they do:

Package For Runs under Returns from validate() src/aegis/validators/detection/ Detect-only Guard PassedResult / FailedResult src/aegis/validators/mutation/ Detect and fix MutationGuard same, plus a mutate()

Pick detection/ if your validator only reports; pick mutation/ if it also repairs the message — but that choice is governed by the Detection vs. Mutation rule: security concerns (XSS, HTML/tag stripping, injection) are detection-only; mutation is for non-adversarial cleanup such as PII redaction or content-quality fixes. (Both are view-based; a MutationValidator is a superset of Validator, so it can also run detect-only under Guard — see Custom Validators.)

docs.title: Simple validator — one module
docs.text:
A self-contained validator is a single snake_case module:

src/aegis/validators/detection/length_validator.py   ->  class LengthValidator

docs.title: Complex validator — one package folder
docs.text:
When a validator needs helpers, pattern tables, or prompt templates, make it a package folder. The public class lives in a _-prefixed private module and is re-exported from the folder's __init__.py; internal helpers stay _-prefixed so the import surface is just the public class:

src/aegis/validators/mutation/input_sanitizer/
├── __init__.py          # re-exports InputSanitizer (the ONLY public symbol)
├── _sanitizer.py        # class InputSanitizer(BaseMutationValidator)
├── _preprocessor.py     # internal helper
└── patterns/            # nested sub-package when helpers group up
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── _xss.py
    └── _sqli.py

# input_sanitizer/__init__.py
from aegis.validators.mutation.input_sanitizer._sanitizer import InputSanitizer

__all__ = ["InputSanitizer"]

Rule of thumb: start with one file; promote to a folder only when helpers appear. Keep the public surface to the validator class — everything else is _-private.

docs.title: Registering the validator
docs.text:
Aegis does not auto-detect validators — you register each one explicitly. For a simple, broadly useful validator that's a single re-export from its category package:

  1. Add your class to the category package's __init__.py and its __all__:

    # src/aegis/validators/detection/__init__.py
from aegis.validators.detection.length_validator import LengthValidator

__all__ = ["LengthValidator"]

  2. It's now importable from its category package — detection or mutation:

    from aegis.validators.detection import LengthValidator

    The category segment is deliberate: the import path itself tells the reader whether a validator is detect-only (detection) or detect-and-fix (mutation). Concrete validators are not aggregated up to the package root — the aegis and aegis.validators roots export only the contract (protocols, base classes, result types), so importing the contract never pulls in every validator's dependencies.

  3. Users register it at runtime with the fluent .use() API:

    from aegis import Guard
from aegis.validators.detection import LengthValidator

guard = Guard("input").use(LengthValidator(max_length=500))

Heavy or niche validators: import from the leaf module

Keep the category __init__.py re-exports to simple, broadly useful, non-LLM validators — importing aegis.validators.detection eagerly loads everything it re-exports. A validator with heavy or optional dependencies (an LLM client, large pattern corpora) should not be re-exported from the category __all__; leave it importable only from its own leaf module so the import cost is paid on demand:

from aegis.validators.detection.scope_check import ScopeCheck

The registration mechanics are otherwise identical, and it still runs under Guard / MutationGuard the same way.

docs.title: Error codes and messages
docs.text:
A FailedResult carries an error_code (callers branch on it), an error_message (what the guard logs on on_fail=LOG), and a details mapping (the specifics) — the validator's public output contract. Consistency across all validators isn't enforced, and that's fine; but within one validator the same failure must always produce the same code, message shape, and details keys.

Codes — stable and machine-readable:

  • One code per distinct failure, specific (TOO_LONG) not generic (VALIDATION_FAILED). SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE; optionally domain-prefixed (LENGTH_TOO_LONG) to stay unique across validators.
  • Define each once as a class constant or Enum — the single source of truth shared by validate(), the tests, and the doc page.
  • A released code is a contract: add a new one, never rename or repurpose it.

Messages — one fixed template per code; keep the variable specifics in details, not baked into prose. The log already records the validator's name, so don't repeat it. Never echo a raw value that could be secret or personal — report a safe summary (length, count, redacted marker) in details.

from typing import Final

from aegis import BaseValidator, FailedResult, PassedResult


class LengthValidator(BaseValidator):
    TOO_LONG: Final = "TOO_LONG"  # define codes once, in one place

    def __init__(self, max_length: int) -> None:
        self.max_length = max_length

    async def validate(self, view, metadata=None):
        value = view.render()
        length = len(value)  # a safe summary — never the raw value
        if length > self.max_length:
            return FailedResult(
                error_code=self.TOO_LONG,
                error_message=f"Value exceeds the {self.max_length}-character limit.",
                details={"length": length, "limit": self.max_length},
            )
        return PassedResult()

Every code gets a row in the doc page's Error Codes table and every details key a row in Failure Details (see Documentation), so the contract stays discoverable without reading the source.

docs.title: Data files
docs.text:
If a validator needs bundled data (word lists, terminology maps, pattern corpora), centralize it rather than scattering per-validator data directories:

  • Put data under src/aegis/data/ and load it through a single path-hardened accessor that validates against path traversal and symlink escape (resolve to an absolute path, confirm it stays within the data root).
  • Never read from a caller-supplied path without validating it.

Bundled data must be clearable

Before adding any data file, make sure it is redistributable under a license compatible with the project's, and free of confidential or personal (PII) data — data you don't have the right to publish can block a release. The library ships no data accessor yet; the first data-backed validator introduces it, following this convention.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Tests mirror the source tree under tests/validators/:

src/aegis/validators/detection/length_validator.py
tests/validators/detection/test_length_validator.py

Folder-based validators mirror the folder:

tests/validators/mutation/input_sanitizer/test_sanitizer.py
  • Tests are async — the suite runs with asyncio_mode = "auto" (pytest-asyncio), so just write async def test_... and drive the validator through a Guard / MutationGuard.
  • Cover, at minimum: a clean value passes, a violating value fails with the expected error_code, boundary conditions, and malformed / empty-string input.
from aegis import Guard
from aegis.validators.detection import LengthValidator

async def test_length_validator_blocks_long_input():
    guard = Guard("test").use(LengthValidator(max_length=5))
    result = await guard.validate("way too long")
    assert result.has_failures
    assert result.failures[0].error_code == "TOO_LONG"

async def test_length_validator_passes_short_input():
    guard = Guard("test").use(LengthValidator(max_length=5))
    result = await guard.validate("ok")
    assert not result.has_failures

See Custom Validators — Testing for the base patterns.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Every validator ships a doc page in the same PR as the code. Two edits:

  1. Add a page at docs/validators/detection/<name>.md or docs/validators/mutation/<name>.md (hyphenated filename, e.g. length-validator.md). Use this template:

    # ValidatorName

One-line tagline — the single thing this validator guards against.

## Description

A short paragraph orienting the reader: what the validator checks and why, when to reach
for it, and whether it is detect-only (runs under `Guard`) or detect-and-fix (runs under
`MutationGuard`). Call out any notable behavior or limits. Keep it general — enough for a
reader to tell whether this is the validator they need, not a full specification.

## Constructor Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max_length` | `int` | — | Maximum allowed length. |

## Usage

```python
from aegis import Guard
from aegis.validators.detection import ValidatorName

guard = Guard("input").use(ValidatorName(...))
result = await guard.validate("...")
```

## Error Codes

| Error Code | Condition |
|---|---|
| `TOO_LONG` | Value exceeds `max_length`. |

## Failure Details

Fields populated on `FailedResult.details`:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `length` | `int` | Actual length of the offending value. |

## API Reference

::: aegis.validators.detection.ValidatorName

    The ::: aegis.validators.detection.ValidatorName line is an mkdocstrings directive — it auto-renders the class's API from its docstrings, so write Google-style docstrings on the class and its __init__. Use the dotted path the validator is actually importable from: the category package for re-exported validators (above), or the leaf module (aegis.validators.detection.scope_check.ScopeCheck) for heavy ones.

  2. Wire it into the nav in mkdocs.yml under the Validators: section, and add a row to the overview table in docs/validators/index.md.

docs.title: Contributor checklist
docs.text:
Before opening the PR:

  • [ ] Researched and spec'd — domain and any governing standards researched up front; the spec captured in the class/module docstring (kept current with the code).
  • [ ] Implements the contract — correct validate() / mutate() signature and return types.
  • [ ] In the right package (detection/ vs mutation/); simple = file, complex = folder with _-private helpers.
  • [ ] Registered in the category __init__.py + __all__.
  • [ ] Every FailedResult has a stable, specific error_code (e.g. TOO_LONG, not VALIDATION_FAILED), defined once as a constant/Enum; each code has a consistent message and details keys (see Error codes and messages).
  • [ ] Tests mirror the source tree and cover boundaries, error paths, and bad input.
  • [ ] Doc page added (using the template) + mkdocs.yml nav entry + docs/validators/index.md row.
  • [ ] CHANGELOG.md updated.
  • [ ] ruff check ., ruff format ., pyright, and pytest all clean.
  • [ ] Peer reviewed.

docs.title: ContentFilter
docs.text: Reject text that contains any of a configured list of blocked terms or phrases.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
ContentFilter is a deterministic, text-only, detect-only validator. It runs under Guard as a policy guardrail on agent input or output, scanning the text for a caller-configured list of literal terms and rejecting it when any term appears. Reach for it when you have a known list of words or phrases to keep out — a competitor list, banned subjects, jailbreak markers, or internal code-names.

Matching is literal, never semantic. Each term is matched as escaped literal text, so the validator finds the exact terms you configure — not a paraphrase, a synonym, a translation, or text that is merely about the subject. Deciding whether text is about a topic without using the words needs a model-backed classifier, which is a separate validator.

By default a term matches only as a discrete word or phrase, on word boundaries. This avoids the Scunthorpe problem — the classic false positive where a clean word is blocked because a banned string appears inside it. Blocking politics does not reject apolitical; blocking cat does not reject category. The trade-off is that a term embedded inside a longer run of characters is not matched. The boundaries are Python re word-character (\w) boundaries, an approximation of Unicode UAX #29 — reliable for space-delimited scripts. A language that does not delimit words with spaces (Chinese, Thai) needs word_boundary=False, which matches anywhere in the text.

Normalization is off by default (opt in with normalize=True): matching is fully literal unless you enable it, which mirrors the engine's off-by-default Guard(normalize=...) and keeps matching predictable. When enabled, it folds cheap cosmetic evasions — case changes, added whitespace, zero-width/invisible characters, and NFKC-compatibility variants such as full-width letters (ｇａｍｂｌｉｎｇ → gambling) — by normalizing both the text and every term before matching. These folds are script-safe: they never map homoglyphs (an engine-only concern), so genuine non-Latin letters are not rewritten to ASCII.

It is not a general safety net, and by design it does not catch:

  • text that is about a blocked subject but never uses a configured term (semantic disclosure);
  • confusable look-alike substitution (Cyrillic о for ASCII o), leetspeak (p0litics), or Base64/hex-encoded terms (documented residual gaps, addressed by future additive hardening);
  • a term split across separately validated messages or chunks.

Each of those belongs to a different single-concern validator. A PASS certifies only that none of the configured terms appeared — never that the text is on-topic, safe, or lawful. Per OWASP, a denylist is not a general security boundary.

On a hit the FailedResult carries only safe summary metadata (an opaque term index, a match count, and an offset); it never echoes the surrounding input. The literal blocked term is included only when report_matched_topic=True, which is off by default in case a term is a confidential code-name. If you enable it, or log the failure details, keep confidential values out of blocked_topics.

docs.title: Constructor Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description blocked_topics list[str] (required) The literal terms/phrases to keep out of the text. At least one is required; each is matched as literal text, never as a regex or a semantic subject. word_boundary bool True When True, match only discrete words/phrases on word boundaries (avoids the Scunthorpe false positive). Set False for substring matching — required for Chinese/Thai and other scripts without word delimiters. case_sensitive bool False When True, skip case-folding. Only takes effect when normalize=True (case-folding is one step of normalization). normalize bool False Opt in to normalize both the text and every term before matching — Unicode normalization, strip zero-width/format characters, collapse whitespace, and case-fold (unless case_sensitive). Off by default: matching is fully literal unless enabled. compatibility_folding bool True Only when normalize=True. True uses NFKC, folding full-width and other compatibility variants (catches a real evasion). False uses canonical NFC, avoiding NFKC over-folding but no longer catching full-width forms. report_matched_topic bool False When True, include the literal matched_topic in the failure details. Off by default because a configured term could be confidential; the surrounding input is never echoed either way. max_input_chars int \| None None Optional resource valve. When set and the rendered text exceeds it, reject with CONTENT_FILTER_INPUT_TOO_LARGE rather than scan. A hard input-size limit belongs to a dedicated length/size validator; this is only a safety valve.

Construction raises ValueError when blocked_topics is a single string instead of a list (a bare string would expand into one-character terms), when blocked_topics is empty, when any term is empty/whitespace-only or empty after normalization (an empty needle matches everything), or when max_input_chars is negative.

The defaults suit space-delimited scripts and literal matching. Enable normalize=True for cosmetic-evasion resistance, and calibrate word_boundary and compatibility_folding against your target languages and your own benign and adversarial text before production.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
The minimal setup blocks a list of words with the safe defaults — word-boundary matching, normalization off (fully literal), nothing echoed:

from aegis import Guard
from aegis.validators.detection import ContentFilter

guard = Guard("input").use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=["gambling", "credit card"]))

result = await guard.validate("Come learn about gambling strategies!")
if result.has_failures:
    print(result.failures[0].error_code)  # CONTENT_BLOCKED

For a Chinese/Thai term, or a deliberate substring policy, opt into substring matching:

guard = Guard("input").use(
    ContentFilter(blocked_topics=["赌博"], word_boundary=False)
)

result = await guard.validate("这里有很多赌博相关的内容。")
if result.has_failures:
    print(result.failures[0].error_code)  # CONTENT_BLOCKED

When more than one term matches, the single reported verdict follows a fixed precedence: CONTENT_FILTER_INPUT_TOO_LARGE → CONTENT_BLOCKED. Within CONTENT_BLOCKED, the earliest matching offset wins (ties broken by the term's index in blocked_topics), and match_count reports how many distinct terms matched.

docs.title: Error Codes
docs.text: Error Code Condition CONTENT_BLOCKED A configured term appears in the text (as a word-boundary match by default, or anywhere in substring mode). CONTENT_FILTER_INPUT_TOO_LARGE max_input_chars is set and the rendered text exceeds it.

docs.title: Failure Details
docs.text:
Fields populated on FailedResult.details. They are safe summaries only — never the surrounding input. match_offset indexes the normalized text and is diagnostic only, since the text is never echoed.

Field Type Description matched_index int Opaque index of the matched term within blocked_topics. Reveals nothing about the content. match_count int How many distinct configured terms matched at least once. match_offset int Character offset of the reported match in the normalized text. word_boundary bool Whether word-boundary matching was in effect. matched_topic str The literal blocked term — present only when report_matched_topic=True. length int Length of the rejected text (only on CONTENT_FILTER_INPUT_TOO_LARGE). limit int The configured max_input_chars (only on CONTENT_FILTER_INPUT_TOO_LARGE).

Bases: BaseValidator

Rejects text that contains any of a configured list of blocked terms or phrases.

A deterministic, text-only, detect-only validator. It runs under Guard and scans a piece of text for a caller-configured list of literal terms/phrases, rejecting the text when any term appears as a normalized, word-boundary match (substring matching is opt-in via word_boundary=False). Reach for it as a policy guardrail on agent input or output when you have a known list of words/phrases to keep out — a competitor list, banned subjects, jailbreak markers, internal code-names.

Matching is literal, never semantic. Each term is matched as escaped literal text — so C++ and a.b match literally, never as a regex — and the validator finds only the exact terms you give it, not a paraphrase, synonym, or translation, and not text that is merely about the subject. Judging whether text is about a topic is the job of a separate, model-backed classifier.

By default a term matches only as a discrete word or phrase, on word boundaries. This avoids the Scunthorpe false positive — blocking politics does not reject apolitical — at the cost of missing a term embedded without delimiters. The boundaries are Python re word-character (\w) boundaries, an approximation of Unicode UAX #29, so a language such as Chinese or Thai that does not delimit words with spaces needs word_boundary=False.

Normalization (off by default; opt in with normalize=True) folds cheap cosmetic evasions — case changes, added whitespace, zero-width/invisible characters, and NFKC-compatibility variants such as full-width letters — by normalizing both the text and every term before matching. It does not fold confusable look-alikes, decode Base64/hex, or reverse leetspeak; those are documented residual gaps handled by future, additive hardening (see the ADR).

Out of scope by design (each is a separate single-concern validator): semantic topic classification, deliberate-obfuscation detection (homoglyphs, leetspeak), encoding/decoding, toxicity/profanity scoring, PII/secret detection, and redacting the term instead of rejecting.

On a hit it returns a FailedResult whose error_message and details carry only safe metadata — an opaque term index, a match count, and an offset — and never the surrounding input. The literal term is included only when report_matched_topic=True (off by default, in case a term is confidential).

Example

from aegis import Guard guard = Guard("input").use(ContentFilter(blocked_topics=["gambling"])) result = await guard.validate("Come learn about gambling strategies!") result.failures[0].error_code 'CONTENT_BLOCKED'
