    blocked_topics: list[str],
    *,
    word_boundary: bool = True,
    case_sensitive: bool = False,
    normalize: bool = False,
    compatibility_folding: bool = True,
    report_matched_topic: bool = False,
    max_input_chars: int | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Configure the blocked terms and matching behavior.

    Args:
        blocked_topics: The literal terms/phrases to keep out of the text. At least one is
            required, and none may be empty or whitespace-only. Each is matched as literal text
            (regex metacharacters are escaped), never as a pattern or a semantic subject.
        word_boundary: When ``True`` (default), a term matches only as a discrete word/phrase on
            word boundaries, avoiding the Scunthorpe false positive (``politics`` does not match
            ``apolitical``). Set ``False`` for substring matching — required for languages that
            do not delimit words with spaces (Chinese, Thai), where word boundaries are
            unreliable, or for a deliberate substring policy.
        case_sensitive: When ``True``, skip case-folding during normalization. Only takes effect
            when ``normalize=True`` — case-folding is one step of normalization, so with
            ``normalize=False`` matching is fully literal regardless of this flag.
        normalize: When ``True``, normalize both the text and every term before matching —
            Unicode normalization, strip zero-width/format characters, collapse whitespace, and
            case-fold (unless ``case_sensitive``). Defeats cheap cosmetic evasions at the cost
            of some strictness. Defaults to ``False`` (matching is fully literal): opt in
            deliberately, mirroring the engine's off-by-default ``Guard(normalize=...)`` so
            normalization is never applied silently. The folds here are script-safe — they
            never map homoglyphs (that stays an engine-only concern, ``Guard(normalize=True)``),
            so genuine non-Latin letters are not rewritten to ASCII.
        compatibility_folding: Only takes effect when ``normalize=True``. When ``True`` (default),
            use NFKC, which folds full-width and other compatibility variants (``ｇａｍｂｌｉｎｇ`` →
            ``gambling``) — a real, documented evasion. When ``False``, use canonical NFC instead,
            which avoids the UAX #15 over-folding risk but no longer catches full-width forms.
        report_matched_topic: When ``True``, include the literal ``matched_topic`` in the failure
            ``details`` (restores the 0.1.0 proof-of-concept field). Off by default because a
            configured term could be a confidential code-name; the surrounding input is never
            echoed either way.
        max_input_chars: Optional resource valve. When set and the rendered text exceeds it, the
            text is rejected with ``CONTENT_FILTER_INPUT_TOO_LARGE`` rather than scanned. Off by
            default — a hard input-size limit belongs to a dedicated length/size validator; this
            is only a safety valve.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``blocked_topics`` is a single string rather than a list (a bare string
            would expand into one-character terms); if ``blocked_topics`` is empty; if any term
            is empty or whitespace-only (an empty needle matches every input and would block
            everything); if any term is empty after normalization; or if ``max_input_chars`` is
            negative (a negative limit exceeds even empty text, so it would reject everything).
    """
    # A bare string is itself iterable, so list("politics") would silently expand to
    # ["p", "o", "l", ...] — one-character terms that over-block almost everything. The
    # list[str] hint is not enforced at runtime (a value from config or JSON can still arrive
    # as a str), so reject it explicitly and fail fast rather than misbehave.
    if isinstance(blocked_topics, str):
        raise ValueError("blocked_topics must be a list of strings, not a single string.")

    topics = list(blocked_topics)

    # Fail closed: with nothing to match against, the validator would silently pass every input —
    # a false sense of security. Reject at construction rather than pass everything.
    if not topics:
        raise ValueError("ContentFilter requires at least one blocked topic in blocked_topics.")

    # An empty or whitespace-only needle is contained in every possible text, so it would reject
    # all input — the documented LLM Guard empty-string bug. Reject it here, reporting the index
    # never the value, in case the value is a confidential term.
    for index, topic in enumerate(topics):
        if not topic.strip():
            raise ValueError(f"blocked_topics[{index}] is empty or whitespace-only.")

    if max_input_chars is not None and max_input_chars < 0:
        # A negative limit makes len(text) > limit true for every candidate — even empty text —
        # so it would reject everything with an impossible bound. Guard it like a real control.
        # (0 is allowed: it means "reject any non-empty text".)
        raise ValueError(f"max_input_chars must be non-negative, got {max_input_chars}.")

    self._word_boundary = word_boundary
    self._report_matched_topic = report_matched_topic
    self._max_input_chars = max_input_chars

    # Build the normalization profile once. ``None`` means "no normalization" — matching is
    # fully literal. Otherwise the script-safe matching profile (NFKC/NFC + strip format chars
    # + collapse whitespace + casefold); compatibility_folding and case_sensitive only take
    # effect here, which is why they are documented as no-ops when normalize is off.
    self._norm_config = (
        NormalizationConfig.for_validators(
            compatibility_folding=compatibility_folding,
            case_sensitive=case_sensitive,
        )
        if normalize
        else None
    )

    # Normalize every term once here, not on each validate() call, since the term list is fixed
    # for the validator's lifetime. A term can survive the empty/whitespace check above yet
    # normalize to nothing (e.g. it was made entirely of zero-width format characters), which
    # would again be a match-everything needle — reject that too, at the one place terms are
    # built. Compile the word-boundary pattern per term now so validate() only runs the search.
    self._blocked: list[_Blocked] = []
    for index, topic in enumerate(topics):
        normalized = self._normalize_text(topic)
        if not normalized:
            raise ValueError(f"blocked_topics[{index}] is empty after normalization.")
        self._blocked.append(
            _Blocked(
                reference_index=index,
                raw=topic,
                normalized=normalized,
                pattern=self._compile_boundary_pattern(normalized) if word_boundary else None,
            )
        )

async def validate(
    self,
    view: ContentView,
    metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
) -> ValidationResult:
    """Inspect the text and report whether it contains any blocked term.

    Scans ``view.render()`` — the whole text, so a Markdown/JSON/code wrapper earns no
    exemption. Since ``render()`` joins parts with a newline, a term spanning a part boundary is
    caught only when that boundary is a whitespace break; a mid-token split is a residual miss
    (see the ADR).

    Returns the single highest-precedence failure (``CONTENT_FILTER_INPUT_TOO_LARGE`` →
    ``CONTENT_BLOCKED``), or ``PassedResult`` if no term matched.

    Args:
        view: The text to inspect as a :class:`ContentView`. Never ``None``; may be empty.
        metadata: Surrounding agent context. Not read by this validator; may be ``None``.

    Returns:
        ``PassedResult`` with ``details = {"terms_checked", "word_boundary"}`` when no term
        matched, or a ``FailedResult`` carrying the ``CONTENT_BLOCKED`` code and a safe-summary
        ``details`` mapping (no surrounding input; the literal term only when
        ``report_matched_topic=True``).
    """
    raw_text = view.render()

    # The size valve runs first: it is both the highest-precedence failure and the point of the
    # cap — reject an oversized candidate before doing any scanning work.
    if self._max_input_chars is not None and len(raw_text) > self._max_input_chars:
        return FailedResult(
            error_code=self.CONTENT_FILTER_INPUT_TOO_LARGE,
            error_message=f"Text exceeds the {self._max_input_chars}-character inspection limit.",
            details={"length": len(raw_text), "limit": self._max_input_chars},
        )

    # Nothing can match in empty or whitespace-only text.
    if not raw_text.strip():
        return self._passed()

    norm_text = self._normalize_text(raw_text)

    # Scan every term and collect the earliest offset each matching term hits at. match_count is
    # the number of *distinct* configured terms that matched at least once — a count, never a
    # list of snippets — and _select picks the single reported verdict deterministically.
    matches = [match for item in self._blocked if (match := self._find(item, norm_text)) is not None]
    winner = self._select(matches)
    if winner is not None:
        return self._to_failure(winner, match_count=len(matches))

    return self._passed()

docs.text: Flag input that would begin a spreadsheet formula if written into a CSV/TSV cell (CSV injection).

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
FormulaInjectionDetector is a deterministic, text-only, detect-only validator. It runs under Guard and reports a failure when a content item, written into a spreadsheet-imported cell (CSV, TSV, and the like), would begin a formula and execute when the file is opened — =cmd|'/C calc'!A0, =HYPERLINK(...). It never changes the content. Reach for it on input or model output that could later be exported to a spreadsheet.

"CSV injection" (CWE-1236 / OWASP) is the common alias. The check is about a formula initiator at a cell's start, not about CSV structure, so the validator is named for the payload rather than the transport; CSV structural injection (forging columns/rows) is a separate concern.

Guard runs its registered validators concurrently, so a failure here does not short-circuit or skip other validators.

docs.title: Obfuscation is decoded before detection
docs.text: Real payloads hide behind encoding layers, so each item is preprocessed before inspection: invisible/zero-width control characters are stripped, then URL-percent, HTML-entity, JavaScript \uXXXX/\xXX, and CSS \3C escapes are decoded repeatedly until the text stops changing (bounded). Without this, %3Dcmd or =cmd would hide the leading =. Preprocessing does not NFKC-fold, so the full-width initiators ＝＋－＠ are matched explicitly. Both passes can be disabled via the constructor when the input's encoding is fully trusted.

docs.title: What it flags
docs.text:
For each cell candidate the validator decodes obfuscation, skips one optional leading structural " and any leading padding (spaces, NBSP, zero-width, …), then inspects the effective start:

  • ascii — a leading =, +, -, or @ (CWE-1236 / OWASP). The default safety floor; narrowable via ascii_triggers.
  • fullwidth — a leading full-width initiator ＝＋－＠ (OWASP), matched explicitly.
  • control — a leading TAB, CR, or LF (OWASP). A control prefix is itself a trigger, so it is never treated as padding.

Any leading trigger flags — there is no numeric, function-name, or handle exception (no universal safe-suffix grammar exists), so -5, +1 650 555 0100, and @mention fail by default. A leading ' (the spreadsheet neutralizer) passes. On a hit, the formula_shape detail names a recognized high-impact shape (dde_pipe_bang, hyperlink, dde) so a caller can raise severity on it.

formula_shape is a best-effort lexical hint, not a formula parser. A recognized shape can over-match a look-alike token inside a string literal (="not really HYPERLINK("). A value of unknown means none of the three recognized shapes matched — it is not a safety signal: other dangerous formulas, including exfiltration functions like =WEBSERVICE(...) and =IMPORTXML(...), report unknown. Use a recognized shape to raise severity; never treat unknown as safe. The marker never changes the verdict, which is already a failure.

All patterns are linear (no nested quantifier that can backtrack), so the validator adds no ReDoS surface of its own.

docs.title: The safety ceiling — read before you rely on this
docs.text:
This validator is defense-in-depth, not a primary control. The authoritative fix is neutralization at the CSV serializer, using a consumer-specific text neutralizer such as a leading ' where the opening application supports it. Ordinary CSV quoting and escaping are not enough: they keep the field structurally intact, but a quoted value like "=1+1" still evaluates as a formula when the file is opened. A guardrail cannot know whether the text will ever become a spreadsheet cell; a passed result means "no leading formula initiator under this policy", never "safe in every spreadsheet".

On general prose the strict policy's false-positive rate is high — -, +, and @ begin ordinary text constantly. This is the accepted default cost; narrow ascii_triggers (e.g. to "=") for prose-heavy deployments, or use formula_shape to raise severity on a recognized command shape.

            a hit, recorded in ``details`` to raise severity on a recognized shape. A best-effort
            lexical match that can over-report a look-alike token; ``"unknown"`` means no recognized
            shape matched, not that the formula is safe. Never changes the verdict.
        strip_invisible_chars: Strip zero-width/control characters before matching.
        decode_obfuscation: Decode URL/HTML/JS/CSS encoding layers before matching.
        max_input_chars: Resource valve. When the rendered view exceeds it, the input is rejected
            with ``FORMULA_INJECTION_INPUT_TOO_LARGE`` rather than preprocessed and scanned,
            bounding the per-request work (up to ``MAX_DECODE_ITERATIONS`` decode passes per item
            plus a per-character category scan). Defaults to 1 MiB of characters; pass ``None`` to
            lift the cap when the input size is already trusted.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``ascii_triggers`` is empty or contains a character outside ``=+-@``, or
            if ``max_input_chars`` is negative.
    """
    # Fail-closed: validate every argument before setting any attribute, so a misconfigured
    # detector raises at construction rather than silently under-enforcing at validate time.
    if not ascii_triggers:
        raise ValueError("ascii_triggers must not be empty; the ASCII safety floor cannot be disabled.")
    invalid = set(ascii_triggers) - _ASCII_TRIGGERS.keys()
    if invalid:
        raise ValueError(f"ascii_triggers may only contain =, +, -, @; got invalid {sorted(invalid)!r}.")
    if max_input_chars is not None and max_input_chars < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"max_input_chars must be non-negative, got {max_input_chars}.")
    self._ascii_triggers = frozenset(ascii_triggers)
    self.detect_fullwidth = detect_fullwidth
    self.detect_control_prefix = detect_control_prefix
    self.skip_leading_padding = skip_leading_padding
    self.skip_leading_quote = skip_leading_quote
    self.detect_formula_shape = detect_formula_shape
    self.strip_invisible_chars = strip_invisible_chars
    self.decode_obfuscation = decode_obfuscation
    self._max_input_chars = max_input_chars

async def validate(
    self,
    view: ContentView,
    metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
) -> ValidationResult:
    """Report whether any content item begins with a spreadsheet formula initiator.

    Inspects each ``ContentItem`` in ``view.items`` as one cell candidate (see the module
    docstring for why this is per-item, not over the flattened ``view.render()``). The resource
    valve measures the rendered length first (the item lengths plus the newline joiners
    ``render()`` would add), before any decoding, so oversized input is rejected without doing the
    per-item decode/scan work — and without materializing the joined string, which the per-item
    scan never needs.

    Args:
        view: The content under inspection. Never ``None``, but may be empty.
        metadata: Surrounding agent context. Optional and unused here.

    Returns:
        ``PassedResult`` when no item's effective start is an enabled trigger. Otherwise a
        ``FailedResult`` carrying ``FORMULA_INJECTION_DETECTED`` for the earliest offending item
        (lowest ``item_index``), with ``details`` holding ``trigger_class``
        (``ascii``/``fullwidth``/``control``), ``trigger`` (the fixed enum, e.g. ``EQUALS``),
        ``match_offset`` (the effective-start position in code points into the decoded item text),
        ``padding_skipped`` (count), ``item_index``, and ``formula_shape``
        (``dde``/``hyperlink``/``dde_pipe_bang``/``unknown``). Or ``FORMULA_INJECTION_INPUT_TOO_LARGE``
        when ``max_input_chars`` is set and the rendered view exceeds it. The raw input, the
        matched cell, and any formula text are never echoed — only the fixed enums, offset, and
        counts are reported.
    """
    # Resource valve. render() joins items with "\n", so the rendered length is the sum of the
    # item lengths plus one "\n" per gap — we compute that directly instead of materializing the
    # whole joined string, which this validator never needs (it scans each item's own value,
    # below). When the cap is lifted (None) we skip the measurement entirely.
    if self._max_input_chars is not None:
        rendered_length = sum(len(item.value) for item in view.items)
        if view.items:
            rendered_length += len(view.items) - 1  # the "\n" joiners render() would insert
        if rendered_length > self._max_input_chars:
            return FailedResult(
                error_message=f"Text exceeds the {self._max_input_chars}-character inspection limit.",
                error_code=self.FORMULA_INJECTION_INPUT_TOO_LARGE,
                details={"length": rendered_length, "limit": self._max_input_chars},
            )

    # The earliest offending item wins: items are scanned in order and the first hit is returned,
    # so the reported item_index is the lowest offending one. Each item is a single cell candidate
    # with one effective start, so exactly one trigger is ever reported — the output stays minimal
    # and never maps out the whole payload.
    for item_index, item in enumerate(view.items):
        hit = _scan_item(
            item.value,
            ascii_triggers=self._ascii_triggers,
            detect_fullwidth=self.detect_fullwidth,
            detect_control_prefix=self.detect_control_prefix,
            skip_leading_padding=self.skip_leading_padding,
            skip_leading_quote=self.skip_leading_quote,
            detect_formula_shape=self.detect_formula_shape,
            strip_invisible=self.strip_invisible_chars,
            decode=self.decode_obfuscation,
        )
        if hit is not None:
            return FailedResult(
                error_message=(
                    f"A content item's effective start is a formula initiator ({hit.trigger_class}) "
                    f"at offset {hit.match_offset}."
                ),
                error_code=self.FORMULA_INJECTION_DETECTED,
                details={
                    "trigger_class": hit.trigger_class,
                    "trigger": hit.trigger,
                    "match_offset": hit.match_offset,
                    "padding_skipped": hit.padding_skipped,
                    "item_index": item_index,
                    "formula_shape": hit.formula_shape,
                },
            )
    return PassedResult()

docs.text: Reject text whose character length falls outside a configured range.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
LengthValidator is a deterministic, text-only, detect-only validator. It runs under Guard and rejects a message whose rendered character length is below min_length or above max_length. Use it as a cheap check that enforces a floor (reject near-empty input) and/or a ceiling (reject oversized input).

Guard runs its registered validators concurrently, so a failure here does not short-circuit or skip other validators — "cheap" refers to this validator's own cost, not to gating the ones registered after it.

Length here means Unicode code points (len(str)), not bytes or grapheme clusters. It measures view.render() — the whole message flattened into one string — so the bound applies across all parts, not per part. Empty input has length 0 and passes only when min_length is 0 (the default).

For a byte ceiling (counting UTF-8 bytes rather than characters), use SizeValidator instead; the two measure different things and are complementary.

result = await guard.validate("x" * 200)

def __init__(self, max_length: int | None = None, min_length: int = 0) -> None:
    """Configure the character-length bounds.

    Args:
        max_length: Maximum allowed length, inclusive. ``None`` (the default) means no ceiling.
            When set, must be a non-negative ``int`` not less than ``min_length``.
        min_length: Minimum required length, inclusive. Defaults to 0 (no floor). Must be a
            non-negative ``int``.

    Raises:
        TypeError: If ``min_length`` is not an ``int``, or if ``max_length`` is neither ``int``
            nor ``None``. The annotations are not enforced at runtime, and a non-int such as
            ``float("nan")`` would slip past the range checks (every comparison with ``nan`` is
            ``False``) and then silently accept all content.
        ValueError: If either bound is negative, or if ``max_length < min_length`` — an empty
            range would reject every input, so it is rejected at construction rather than
            silently failing closed on every call.
    """
    # Reject non-int bounds before comparing: the type annotations are not enforced at
    # runtime, and a float("nan") passes every "< 0" / "<" check (all comparisons with nan
    # are False), which would then make `length > max_length` always False too — silently
    # accepting all content. bool is excluded too: although True/False == 1/0 compare
    # correctly, they leak into the error message ("... > True"), so reject them as a type.
    # max_length also accepts None, meaning "no ceiling" — the length > max check is skipped.
    if not isinstance(min_length, int) or isinstance(min_length, bool):
        raise TypeError(f"min_length must be an int, got {type(min_length).__name__}.")
    if max_length is not None and (not isinstance(max_length, int) or isinstance(max_length, bool)):
        raise TypeError(f"max_length must be an int or None, got {type(max_length).__name__}.")
    if min_length < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"min_length must be non-negative, got {min_length}.")
    if max_length is not None and max_length < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"max_length must be non-negative, got {max_length}.")
    if max_length is not None and max_length < min_length:
        raise ValueError(f"max_length ({max_length}) must be >= min_length ({min_length}).")

    self.min_length = min_length
    self.max_length = max_length

async def validate(
    self,
    view: ContentView,
    metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
) -> ValidationResult:
    """Report whether the rendered content length is within bounds.

    Args:
        view: The content under inspection. Never ``None``; may be empty.
        metadata: Surrounding agent context. Unused — length is self-contained.

    Returns:
        ``PassedResult`` when ``min_length <= length <= max_length``, otherwise a
        ``FailedResult`` carrying ``LENGTH_TOO_SHORT`` or ``LENGTH_EXCEEDED`` and the measured
        length plus the breached bound in ``details``.
    """
    length = len(view.render())

    if length < self.min_length:
        return FailedResult(
            error_message=f"Text too short: {length} < {self.min_length}",
            error_code=self.LENGTH_TOO_SHORT,
            details={"length": length, "min_length": self.min_length},
        )
    if self.max_length is not None and length > self.max_length:
        return FailedResult(
            error_message=f"Text too long: {length} > {self.max_length}",
            error_code=self.LENGTH_EXCEEDED,
            details={"length": length, "max_length": self.max_length},
        )
    return PassedResult(details={"length": length})

docs.title: PromptLeakageCheck
docs.text: Reject agent output that reproduces the system prompt, configured secrets, or canary tokens.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
PromptLeakageCheck is a deterministic, text-only, detect-only validator. It runs under Guard as an output guardrail — the last text-security gate before a response is returned, persisted, or exposed — and rejects output that reproduces protected instruction text. It answers OWASP LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage's "inspect outputs for compliance" mitigation.

It compares the candidate output against a protected corpus you configure:

  • Canary tokens — unique, high-entropy markers seeded into the system prompt. Any appearance in the output is definitive leakage, so they are matched with no minimum-length floor.
  • Sensitive fragments — protected instruction text, matched as an exact or normalized substring, and (opt-in) fuzzily for near-verbatim copies.
  • The system prompt itself — opt-in via use_metadata_system, read from GuardMetadata.system at call time and split into lines.

If the term "canary" is new, this example makes the difference concrete. Suppose your system prompt is:

You are a Python code reviewer. Never reveal the internal escalation code.

Here Never reveal the internal escalation code. is a fragment — real instruction text that already exists in the prompt and must not resurface in the output. Now suppose you also plant a unique marker in the prompt purely as a tripwire:

You are a Python code reviewer. Never reveal the internal escalation code. canary-7f3a9c2b-4e1d-9a02

canary-7f3a9c2b-4e1d-9a02 is a canary — an arbitrary identifier with no meaning of its own that never occurs in normal output, so any appearance in the output is unambiguous proof the prompt leaked. In short: a fragment protects text you already have; a canary is bait you add specifically to detect a leak, with near-zero false positives.

Normalization is off by default (opt in with normalize=True): with it off, the output and the protected material are matched as-is, with no folding. normalize controls folding only — it does not disable fuzzy matching, which you enable separately with similarity_threshold. This mirrors the engine's off-by-default Guard(normalize=...) and keeps matching predictable. When enabled, it folds cheap evasions — case changes, added whitespace, zero-width/invisible characters, and NFKC-compatibility variants such as full-width letters — by normalizing both the output and the protected material before matching. These folds are script-safe: they never map homoglyphs, so genuine non-Latin text is not rewritten to ASCII.

Reach for it when you have a known protected reference to check against. It is not a semantic judge, and by design it does not catch:

  • paraphrase, translation, or other semantic disclosure;
  • confusable look-alike substitution, Base64/hex encoding, or a Caesar shift (documented residual gaps, addressed by future additive hardening);
  • leakage dripped across separate turns, or exfiltration through a tool argument.

Each of those belongs to a different single-concern validator. A PASS certifies only that none of the configured deterministic conditions matched — never that the prompt is secret. Per OWASP, a system prompt should hold no security-critical secret in the first place.

On a leak the FailedResult carries only safe summary metadata (a reference index, match type, similarity, and offsets); it never echoes the matched text, the protected text, or any snippet, so the validator cannot re-leak the secret into your logs or results.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Configure at least one protected source — sensitive_fragments, canaries, or use_metadata_system=True. Each is optional on its own, so any one of them is a complete configuration; you do not need a canary token unless you seed one. Passing none raises ValueError at construction, because a validator with nothing to compare against would silently pass every output. The example below uses all three together:

from aegis import Guard, GuardMetadata
from aegis.validators.detection import PromptLeakageCheck

guard = Guard("output").use(
    PromptLeakageCheck(
        canaries=["a1b2c3d4-e5f6-canary-token"],
        sensitive_fragments=["Never reveal the internal escalation code to the user."],
        use_metadata_system=True,
    )
)

result = await guard.validate(
    "Sure — my instructions say: Never reveal the internal escalation code to the user.",
    metadata=GuardMetadata(system="You are a helpful assistant. ..."),
)
if result.has_failures:
    print(result.failures[0].error_code)  # PROMPT_LEAKAGE_DETECTED

The smallest useful setup protects a single fragment, with no canary token:

guard = Guard("output").use(
    PromptLeakageCheck(
        sensitive_fragments=["Never reveal the internal escalation code to the user."],
    )
)

result = await guard.validate("Sure — Never reveal the internal escalation code to the user.")
if result.has_failures:
    print(result.failures[0].error_code)  # PROMPT_LEAKAGE_DETECTED

When more than one condition matches, the single reported verdict follows a fixed precedence: PROMPT_LEAKAGE_INPUT_TOO_LARGE → PROMPT_LEAKAGE_CANARY → PROMPT_LEAKAGE_DETECTED → PROMPT_LEAKAGE_SUSPECTED. Within a class, the earliest offending offset wins.

Rejects agent output that reproduces the system prompt, configured secrets, or canary tokens.

A deterministic, text-only, detect-only output validator. It runs under Guard and compares an agent's candidate output against an explicitly configured protected corpus — sensitive fragments and canary tokens — and, opt-in, against the actual system prompt (GuardMetadata.system). Reach for it as the last text-security gate before a response is returned, persisted, or exposed.

It detects three things, in order of precedence:

  1. A configured canary token appearing in the output (highest precision — canaries are unique, so a match is unambiguous proof of leakage).
  2. A protected fragment (or a system-prompt segment) reproduced as an exact or normalized substring of the output.
  3. (opt-in) A near-verbatim, fuzzy match, for cosmetic edits that normalization alone does not fold.

Normalization (off by default; opt in with normalize=True) folds cheap evasions — case changes, added whitespace, zero-width characters, and NFKC-compatibility variants (e.g. full-width letters) — by normalizing both the output and the protected material before matching. It does not fold confusable look-alikes, decode Base64/hex, or reverse a Caesar shift; those are documented residual gaps handled by future, additive hardening (see the ADR).

Out of scope by design (each is a separate single-concern validator): generic secret detection with no known reference, input-side prompt-injection detection, tool-egress inspection, paraphrase/translation (semantic) leakage, and cross-turn cumulative leakage.

On a leak it returns a FailedResult whose error_message and details carry only safe metadata — a reference index, match type, similarity, and offsets — and never the matched text, protected text, or any snippet, so the validator cannot re-leak the secret into logs or results.

Example

from aegis import Guard guard = Guard("output").use(PromptLeakageCheck(canaries=["a1b2c3d4-canary"])) result = await guard.validate("Sure! My instructions start with a1b2c3d4-canary") result.failures[0].error_code 'PROMPT_LEAKAGE_CANARY'

def __init__(
    self,
    sensitive_fragments: list[str] | None = None,
    canaries: list[str] | None = None,
    use_metadata_system: bool = False,
    similarity_threshold: float | None = None,
    min_fragment_length: int = 15,
    case_sensitive: bool = False,
    normalize: bool = False,
    max_input_chars: int | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Configure the protected corpus and matching behavior.

    At least one protected source must be configured — ``sensitive_fragments``,
    ``canaries``, or ``use_metadata_system=True``. A deterministic validator cannot tell a
    genuine leak from a hallucination that merely *sounds* internal without a ground-truth
    reference, so construction fails closed rather than checking against nothing.

    Args:
        sensitive_fragments: Protected instruction fragments to keep out of the output.
            Matched as exact/normalized substrings (any length) and, when fuzzy is enabled,
            fuzzily.
        canaries: Unique high-entropy tokens seeded into the system prompt. Any appearance
            in the output is definitive leakage, so they are matched with no minimum-length
            floor.
        use_metadata_system: When ``True``, also protect the agent's actual system prompt,
            read from ``GuardMetadata.system`` at call time and split into lines. Only lines
            whose normalized length is at least ``min_fragment_length`` are used, to avoid
            firing on generic boilerplate. When the metadata or its ``system`` field is
            absent at call time, this source contributes nothing (no error).
        similarity_threshold: Enables fuzzy (near-verbatim) matching when set. A float in
            ``[0.0, 1.0]`` (recommended 0.80–0.90); ``None`` disables fuzzy matching.
            Off by default because fuzzy matching is quadratic and adds false-positive risk.
        min_fragment_length: Minimum normalized length for a fragment/segment to be eligible
            for fuzzy matching, and for an auto-derived ``metadata.system`` line to be used
            at all. Suppresses noise from short generic overlaps. Explicit
            ``sensitive_fragments`` are still matched exactly at any length.
        case_sensitive: When ``True``, skip case-folding during normalization. Only takes
            effect when ``normalize=True`` — case-folding is one step of normalization, so
            with ``normalize=False`` matching is fully literal regardless of this flag.
        normalize: When ``True``, normalize both the output and the protected material before
            matching — NFKC, strip zero-width/format characters, collapse whitespace, and
            case-fold (unless ``case_sensitive``). Defeats cheap cosmetic evasions at the cost
            of some strictness. Defaults to ``False`` (matching is fully literal): opt in
            deliberately, mirroring the engine's off-by-default ``Guard(normalize=...)`` so
            normalization is never applied silently. The folds here are script-safe — they
            never map homoglyphs, so genuine non-Latin text is not rewritten to ASCII.
        max_input_chars: Optional resource valve. When set and the rendered output exceeds
            it, the output is rejected with ``PROMPT_LEAKAGE_INPUT_TOO_LARGE`` rather than
            scanned. Off by default — a hard input-size limit belongs to a dedicated length
            validator; this is only a convenience cap on fuzzy-matching work.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If no protected source is configured; if any ``sensitive_fragments`` or
            ``canaries`` entry is empty or whitespace-only (an empty string is a substring
            of every output and would force a spurious match); if ``similarity_threshold``
            is outside ``[0.0, 1.0]``; if ``min_fragment_length`` is negative; or if
            ``max_input_chars`` is negative.
    """
    fragments = list(sensitive_fragments or [])
    canary_tokens = list(canaries or [])

    # Fail closed: without a ground-truth reference there is nothing to compare against, so
    # this validator would silently pass everything — a false sense of security.
    if not fragments and not canary_tokens and not use_metadata_system:
        raise ValueError(
            "PromptLeakageCheck requires at least one protected source: pass "
            "sensitive_fragments, canaries, or set use_metadata_system=True."
        )

    # An empty or whitespace-only needle is a substring of every possible output, so it
    # would reject all input. Reject it at construction — this is a real gap, not a style
    # choice. (Report the source and index, never the value, in case the value is secret.)
    for index, fragment in enumerate(fragments):
        if not fragment.strip():
            raise ValueError(f"sensitive_fragments[{index}] is empty or whitespace-only.")
    for index, canary in enumerate(canary_tokens):
        if not canary.strip():
            raise ValueError(f"canaries[{index}] is empty or whitespace-only.")

    if similarity_threshold is not None and not 0.0 <= similarity_threshold <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError(f"similarity_threshold must be within [0.0, 1.0], got {similarity_threshold}.")
    if min_fragment_length < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"min_fragment_length must be non-negative, got {min_fragment_length}.")
    if max_input_chars is not None and max_input_chars < 0:
        # A negative limit makes len(output) > limit true for every candidate — even empty
        # output — so it would reject everything with an impossible bound. Guard it like the
        # other numeric controls. (0 is allowed: it means "reject any non-empty output".)
        raise ValueError(f"max_input_chars must be non-negative, got {max_input_chars}.")

    self._use_metadata_system = use_metadata_system
    self._similarity_threshold = similarity_threshold
    self._min_fragment_length = min_fragment_length
    self._normalize = normalize
    self._max_input_chars = max_input_chars

    # Build the normalization profile once. ``None`` means "no normalization" — matching is
    # fully literal. Otherwise the script-safe matching profile (NFKC + strip format chars +
    # collapse whitespace + casefold); this validator always uses NFKC (no compatibility_folding
    # knob) and case_sensitive only takes effect here. ``self._normalize`` is retained because
    # the "normalized" match-type gate in _find_substring reads it.
    self._norm_config = NormalizationConfig.for_validators(case_sensitive=case_sensitive) if normalize else None

    # Canaries and fragments are fixed for the validator's lifetime, so normalize them once
    # here rather than on every validate() call. They live in separate lists because each is
    # checked by a different matcher — canaries by _find_canary, fragments (plus the per-call
    # metadata.system segments) by _find_substring / _find_fuzzy — so each matcher receives
    # exactly the items it checks, with no source filtering. Built after self._norm_config
    # above, which _normalize_text reads.
    self._canaries: list[_Protected] = [
        _Protected(_SOURCE_CANARY, index, canary, self._normalize_text(canary))
        for index, canary in enumerate(canary_tokens)
    ]
    self._fragments: list[_Protected] = [
        _Protected(_SOURCE_FRAGMENT, index, fragment, self._normalize_text(fragment))
        for index, fragment in enumerate(fragments)
    ]

async def validate(
    self,
    view: ContentView,
    metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
) -> ValidationResult:
    """Inspect the candidate output and report whether it leaks protected material.

    Scans ``view.render()`` — the whole candidate, so a Markdown/JSON/code wrapper earns no
    exemption. Since ``render()`` joins parts with a newline, a fragment spanning a part
    boundary is caught only when that boundary is a whitespace break; a mid-token split is a
    residual miss (deferred separator/interleaving handling — see the ADR).

    Returns the single highest-precedence failure (``INPUT_TOO_LARGE`` → ``CANARY`` →
    ``DETECTED`` → ``SUSPECTED``), or ``PassedResult`` if nothing matched.

    Args:
        view: The candidate output as a :class:`ContentView`. Never ``None``; may be empty.
        metadata: Surrounding agent context. Read only when ``use_metadata_system=True``,
            for its ``system`` field. May be ``None``.

    Returns:
        ``PassedResult`` with ``details = {"fragments_checked", "sources", "fuzzy_enabled"}``
        when no configured condition matched, or a ``FailedResult`` carrying a stable
        ``error_code`` and a safe-summary ``details`` mapping (no matched or protected text).
    """
    raw_output = view.render()

    # The size valve runs first: it is both the highest-precedence failure and the point of
    # the cap — reject an oversized candidate before doing any (potentially quadratic) work.
    if self._max_input_chars is not None and len(raw_output) > self._max_input_chars:
        return FailedResult(
            error_code=self.PROMPT_LEAKAGE_INPUT_TOO_LARGE,
            error_message=f"Candidate output exceeds the {self._max_input_chars}-character inspection limit.",
            details={"length": len(raw_output), "limit": self._max_input_chars},
        )

    # Build the fragment targets — the configured fragments plus any per-call metadata.system
    # segments, both matched by _find_substring / _find_fuzzy — before the empty-output check,
    # so a PASS always summarizes the same configured sources whether or not there was content
    # to scan. Canaries need no per-call assembly; they are the static self._canaries list.
    targets = self._build_fragment_targets(metadata)

    # Nothing can have leaked from empty or whitespace-only output.
    if not raw_output.strip():
        return self._passed(self._canaries + targets)

    norm_output = self._normalize_text(raw_output)

    # Check by precedence and short-circuit: a canary match outranks any fragment match,
    # which outranks any fuzzy match, so there is no need to look for a weaker class once a
    # stronger one has fired. Each matcher gets exactly the list it checks — no source filter.
    canary_match = self._find_canary(norm_output, self._canaries)
    if canary_match is not None:
        return self._to_failure(canary_match)

    substring_match = self._find_substring(raw_output, norm_output, targets)
    if substring_match is not None:
        return self._to_failure(substring_match)

    if self._similarity_threshold is not None:
        fuzzy_match = self._find_fuzzy(norm_output, targets)
        if fuzzy_match is not None:
            return self._to_failure(fuzzy_match)

    return self._passed(self._canaries + targets)

docs.text: Reject text that exceeds a UTF-8 byte-size ceiling.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
SizeValidator is a deterministic, text-only, detect-only validator. It runs under Guard and rejects a message whose rendered text exceeds max_size_bytes when encoded as UTF-8. Use it as a cheap check to cap text-payload size at a trust boundary.

Guard runs its registered validators concurrently, so a failure here does not short-circuit or skip other validators — "cheap" refers to this validator's own cost, not to gating the ones registered after it.

Size here means UTF-8 bytes, not characters: a multi-byte character (an emoji, a CJK ideograph) costs more than one byte. It measures the UTF-8 byte length of view.render() — the whole message flattened into one string — so the limit applies across all parts, not per part. The count is total and never raises: text carrying a lone/unpaired surrogate (which a plain UTF-8 encode would reject) is measured via errors="surrogatepass" rather than crashing the guard; whether the text is well-formed Unicode is a separate validator's concern. The default limit is 5 MiB (5,242,880 bytes) of text content. This counts only the rendered text bytes, not request framing or other payload fields, so it is not a drop-in for a servlet request-size limit (Tomcat's maxPostSize, for example, defaults to 2 MiB and governs the whole request body).

For a character-count bound instead, use LengthValidator; the two measure different things and are complementary.

def __init__(self, max_size_bytes: int = DEFAULT_MAX_SIZE_BYTES) -> None:
    """Configure the UTF-8 byte-size ceiling.

    Args:
        max_size_bytes: Maximum allowed size in UTF-8 bytes, inclusive. Must be non-negative;
            0 means "reject any non-empty input".

    Raises:
        TypeError: If ``max_size_bytes`` is not an ``int``. The annotation is not enforced at
            runtime, and a non-int such as ``float("nan")`` would slip past the range check
            (every comparison with ``nan`` is ``False``) and then silently accept all content.
        ValueError: If ``max_size_bytes`` is negative — a negative ceiling would reject every
            input, including empty, so it is rejected at construction.
    """
    # Reject a non-int ceiling before comparing: a float("nan") passes "< 0" (all nan
    # comparisons are False), which would make `size_bytes > max_size_bytes` always False too,
    # silently accepting all content. bool is excluded too: although True/False == 1/0 compare
    # correctly, they leak into the error message ("... > False bytes"), so reject them.
    if not isinstance(max_size_bytes, int) or isinstance(max_size_bytes, bool):
        raise TypeError(f"max_size_bytes must be an int, got {type(max_size_bytes).__name__}.")
    if max_size_bytes < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"max_size_bytes must be non-negative, got {max_size_bytes}.")
    self.max_size_bytes = max_size_bytes

async def validate(
    self,
    view: ContentView,
    metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
) -> ValidationResult:
    """Report whether the rendered content's UTF-8 byte size is within the limit.

    Args:
        view: The content under inspection. Never ``None``; may be empty.
        metadata: Surrounding agent context. Unused — size is self-contained.

    Returns:
        ``PassedResult`` when ``size_bytes <= max_size_bytes``, otherwise a ``FailedResult``
        carrying ``SIZE_EXCEEDED`` and the measured and allowed sizes in ``details``.
    """
    # errors="surrogatepass" keeps the size check total: a str carrying a lone/unpaired
    # surrogate (e.g. produced upstream by errors="surrogateescape" decoding, or by splitting a
    # surrogate pair mid-buffer) would make a plain encode("utf-8") raise UnicodeEncodeError and
    # crash the guard. surrogatepass encodes such a code point as its 3 UTF-8 bytes instead, so
    # malformed text is measured, not thrown on. Whether the text is well-formed is a separate
    # validator's concern — the size gate only counts bytes.
    size_bytes = len(view.render().encode("utf-8", "surrogatepass"))

    if size_bytes > self.max_size_bytes:
        return FailedResult(
            error_message=f"Text size too large: {size_bytes} bytes > {self.max_size_bytes} bytes",
            error_code=self.SIZE_EXCEEDED,
            details={"size_bytes": size_bytes, "max_size_bytes": self.max_size_bytes},
        )
    return PassedResult(details={"size_bytes": size_bytes})

docs.text: Flag text carrying a known SQL-injection construct.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
SqlInjectionDetector is a deterministic, text-only, detect-only validator. It runs under Guard and reports a failure when the content carries a known SQL-injection construct; it never changes the content. Use it as a cheap, non-LLM check at a trust boundary on text that may reach a query layer.

Guard runs its registered validators concurrently, so a failure here does not short-circuit or skip other validators — "cheap" refers to this validator's own cost.

docs.title: Obfuscation is decoded before detection
docs.text: Real payloads hide behind encoding layers, so the rendered content is preprocessed before any pattern runs: invisible/zero-width control characters are stripped, then URL-percent, HTML-entity, JavaScript \uXXXX/\xXX, and CSS \3C escapes are decoded repeatedly until the text stops changing (bounded). Without this, a URL-encoded UNION%20SELECT would sail past a raw-text matcher. Each pass can be disabled via the constructor when the input's encoding is fully trusted.

docs.title: What it flags
docs.text:
The classic query-breaking constructs — not individual metacharacters (a bare ; or ' would drown callers in false positives on ordinary prose):

  • union_select — UNION SELECT / UNION ALL SELECT extraction.
  • stacked_query — a terminator (;) followed by a complete statement: DROP TABLE, DELETE FROM, TRUNCATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE/DATABASE, CREATE TABLE/…, INSERT INTO <t> with a ( / VALUES / SELECT / SET continuation, UPDATE <t> SET <col>=, or EXEC(/EXEC sp_/ EXEC xp_/EXEC schema.proc. Each keyword is anchored to a word boundary and (for the ambiguous forms) a SQL continuation, so English prose after a semicolon (; create your profile, ; delete fromagerie, ; insert into the box) is not flagged.
  • tautology — an always-true equal-operands comparison with OR or AND (boolean-blind): ' OR '1'='1, 0 OR '1'='1', OR 1=1, AND 1=1. A false comparison ('admin'='guest', 1=2, '1'='10') and benign arithmetic (2 or 3 = 5) are not flagged.
  • comment_tail / block_comment — SQL comments: a /* opener, or a --/# tail after a quote or terminator ('--, ; --).
  • time_based_probe — blind probes with a numeric argument: SLEEP(5), pg_sleep(10), BENCHMARK(n,…), or WAITFOR DELAY. (A numeric arg keeps sleep (now) prose from matching.)

Every pattern is linear (no nested quantifier that can backtrack), so the validator adds no ReDoS surface of its own.

docs.text: This validator is defense-in-depth, not a primary control. The authoritative SQL-injection defense is parameterized queries (prepared statements) — never string-concatenated SQL. A passed result means "no known injection marker found", never "provably safe".

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
XxeDetector is a deterministic, text-only, detect-only validator. It runs under Guard and reports a failure when the content carries an XXE-capable XML construct — an external entity, an external or inline DTD, an entity declaration, or XInclude; it never changes the content. Use it as a cheap, non-LLM check at a trust boundary on input (or model output) that could, now or downstream, reach an XML processor.

Guard runs its registered validators concurrently, so a failure here does not short-circuit or skip other validators — "cheap" refers to this validator's own cost.

docs.title: Obfuscation is decoded before detection
docs.text: Real payloads hide behind encoding layers, so the content is preprocessed before any pattern runs: invisible/zero-width control characters are stripped, then URL-percent, HTML-entity, JavaScript \uXXXX/\xXX, and CSS \3C escapes are decoded repeatedly until the text stops changing (bounded). Without this, %3C!DOCTYPE or <!ENTITY would sail past a raw-text matcher. Each pass can be disabled via the constructor when the input's encoding is fully trusted.

docs.title: Declarations inside inert regions are not flagged
docs.text: A declaration written inside a complete comment (<!-- -->), CDATA section (<![CDATA[ ]]>), or processing instruction (<? ?>) is data, not markup — an XML processor never acts on it — so those complete regions are blanked out before the patterns run. This removes the classic "matcher fires on <!DOCTYPE inside a comment" false positive without parsing hostile XML. An unterminated region is treated the opposite way: it cannot make what follows inert, so a construct after an unclosed comment or CDATA is still flagged (fail toward detection).

docs.title: What it flags
docs.text:
Capability-bearing DTD/entity machinery and XInclude — not every < or &:

  • external_entity — an entity declaration (general or % parameter) carrying an external ID: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">, <!ENTITY p PUBLIC "id" "http://host/">. The file-read / SSRF vector.
  • external_dtd — a DOCTYPE pointing at an external subset: <!DOCTYPE foo SYSTEM "foo.dtd">.
  • dtd_internal_subset — a DOCTYPE opening an inline [ ... ] subset, where entity bombs (billion laughs) and internal entities live: <!DOCTYPE foo [ <!ENTITY x "..."> ]>.
  • parameter_entity — a parameter-entity declaration <!ENTITY % ...>, the blind/out-of-band building block.
  • entity_declaration — any other entity declaration, the billion-laughs building block. Presence is the signal; the validator never expands it to classify (CWE-776).
  • xinclude — the XInclude namespace http://www.w3.org/2001/XInclude or an <xi:include> element, which pulls in an external file/URL without a DTD. Matching the namespace URI itself (not just an <xi:include> element) catches a renamed prefix, at the cost of flagging input that merely names the URI — a bare xmlns:xi="…/XInclude" declaration, or prose quoting the spec URL, will trip this. That false positive is intentional (bias to recall). A non-xi prefix bound to the XInclude namespace out of view (an <p:include> element whose xmlns binding sits on an ancestor that is not in the rendered text) is not caught — a limitation of a text scanner that does not resolve namespace scope across a document it may see only in part.
  • bare_doctype — a capability-free bare <!DOCTYPE name>. Only flagged when flag_bare_doctype=True (see below); off by default so a bare HTML5 doctype passes.

Matching is case-insensitive and every pattern is linear (no nested quantifier that can backtrack), so the validator adds no ReDoS surface of its own.

The authoritative XXE defense is a hardened XML parser at the processing site — DTDs disabled, external entities disabled, no external resolution. A passed result means "no known XXE construct found", never "provably safe". Byte-level transport tricks (UTF-16/UTF-32 BOM, base64- or archive-wrapped XML) are out of scope by design: they belong to an upstream decode/extraction stage that hands this validator a decoded string.

async def validate(
    self,
    view: ContentView,
    metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
) -> ValidationResult:
    """Report whether the rendered content carries an XXE-capable construct (after decoding).

    Each item is decoded and inert-masked on its own, then the masked items are flattened through
    ``ContentView.render()`` for matching — so a construct split across an item boundary is still
    caught (``render()`` joins with whitespace, matched by ``\\s``), while an inert region in one
    item cannot mask a construct in another.

    Args:
        view: The content under inspection. Never ``None``, but may be empty.
        metadata: Surrounding agent context. Optional and unused here.

    Returns:
        ``PassedResult`` when no XXE construct is found. Otherwise a ``FailedResult`` carrying
        ``XXE_DETECTED`` with ``details`` locating the first construct — ``match_offset`` and
        ``match_length`` (into the decoded/stripped/masked text that was scanned, **not** the raw
        input, since decoding shifts offsets) and ``construct`` (the construct class, e.g.
        ``"external_entity"``, ``"dtd_internal_subset"``). Or ``XXE_INPUT_TOO_LARGE`` when
        ``max_input_chars`` is set and exceeded. The raw input — and any path, URL, or name
        inside it — is never echoed; only safe summaries are reported.
    """
    # Resource valve first: reject oversized input before any decode/scan. The cap bounds the
    # total text the scan will process — the sum of the item values — so many just-under-limit
    # items cannot blow up the aggregate work. Summing item lengths (rather than measuring
    # ``view.render()``) keeps the valve off render()'s internal format: the separators it places
    # between items are its concern, not work this validator does.
    total_length = sum(len(item.value) for item in view.items)
    if self._max_input_chars is not None and total_length > self._max_input_chars:
        return FailedResult(
            error_message=f"Text exceeds the {self._max_input_chars}-character inspection limit.",
            error_code=self.XXE_INPUT_TOO_LARGE,
            details={"length": total_length, "limit": self._max_input_chars},
        )

    # Decode and inert-mask each item on its own (see _decode_and_mask: one item's inert region
    # must never make another item's construct inert), then let render() flatten the masked
    # items. Delegating the join to the view keeps the scan aligned with however render()
    # flattens it, rather than hardcoding a separator here.
    masked_view = ContentView(items=tuple(self._decode_and_mask(item) for item in view.items))
    scanned = masked_view.render()
    match = _find_xxe(scanned, flag_bare_doctype=self.flag_bare_doctype)
    if match is not None:
        start, end, construct = match
        return FailedResult(
            error_message=f"Input contains an XXE construct ({construct}) at offset {start}.",
            error_code=self.XXE_DETECTED,
            details={"match_offset": start, "match_length": end - start, "construct": construct},
        )
    return PassedResult()

Mutation is supported, with a caveat

Under the Detection vs. Mutation rule, XSS / HTML-stripping is a security concern that normally should detect-and-reject rather than repair. HtmlSanitizer is an exception: it is a thin wrapper over the well-tested nh3/ammonia sanitizer, so repairing content is safe and the mutation path is kept. If you prefer to reject unsafe content outright instead of silently repairing it, run it under Guard (detect-only, blocking on failure).

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
HtmlSanitizer treats each content part as an HTML fragment and enforces an allowlist of tags, attributes, URL schemes, and (optionally) inline-CSS properties. Everything outside the allowlist — <script>, event-handler attributes such as onerror, javascript: URLs, HTML comments, unknown tags — is removed, and the result is re-serialized from a spec-compliant parse tree. It defends against cross-site scripting (CWE-79) and mutation-XSS when agent content may later be rendered as HTML by a downstream client.

It is a detect-and-fix validator: run it under MutationGuard to repair content, or under Guard for detect-only (rejecting anything not already in canonical, allowlisted form). Detection and repair share one definition of safe — a part is acceptable exactly when it already equals its sanitized form — so validate reports a change and mutate emits the sanitized text.

The sanitizer is powered by nh3 (the Rust ammonia library over html5ever). Because it parses input into a tree and re-serializes, it resists syntactic obfuscation: mixed case (<ScRiPt>), HTML entities (javascript:), and malformed nesting are all resolved to the canonical tree before the allowlist is applied.

HTML only — not for plain text

Apply this only to content meant to be rendered as HTML. A stray < or > in plain text (for example 5 < 3) is HTML-escaped, which changes the text and is reported as a violation. Deciding whether content should be HTML at all is the caller's routing decision.

Widening the allowlist enlarges the attack surface

The defaults are safe: HTML-only, tightened URL schemes, inline CSS disabled. Two options are especially load-bearing — adding foreign-content tags (svg, math, foreignObject) reopens namespace-confusion vectors, and enabling inline CSS is only as safe as the property list you allow.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from aegis import MutationGuard
from aegis.validators.mutation import HtmlSanitizer

guard = MutationGuard("output").use(HtmlSanitizer())
result = await guard.validate("<script>alert(1)</script>Hello")

if result.was_mutated:
    print(result.output)  # "Hello"

Enabling inline CSS is opt-in. Start from a vetted property set rather than allowing arbitrary properties, and remember style must also be listed in allowed_attributes:

sanitizer = HtmlSanitizer(
    allowed_tags={"p", "span"},
    allowed_attributes={"p": {"style"}, "span": {"style"}},
    allowed_css_properties={"color", "font-weight", "text-align"},
)

nh3 sanitizes CSS values too — a url() with a disallowed scheme is dropped even on an allowed property. Two residuals are worth knowing. First, behavior and -moz-binding load script through a url() that this value-level filtering does not catch, so do not allowlist them. Second, the legacy IE expression() function is not stripped by nh3, but it is inert in every browser from IE8 (2009) onward and is treated as an accepted out-of-scope non-goal.

Reduces HTML content to a safe, allowlisted subset, removing anything else.

HtmlSanitizer treats each content part as an HTML fragment and enforces an allowlist of tags, attributes, URL schemes, and (optionally) inline-CSS properties. Everything outside the allowlist — <script>, event-handler attributes such as onerror, javascript: URLs, HTML comments, unknown tags — is removed, and the result is re-serialized from a spec-compliant parse tree. This defends against cross-site scripting (XSS, CWE-79) and mutation-XSS when agent content may later be rendered as HTML by a downstream client.

It is a detect-and-fix validator. Under MutationGuard it repairs content; under Guard it runs detect-only (rejecting anything not already in canonical, allowlisted form). Detection and repair share one definition of "safe": a part is acceptable exactly when it already equals its sanitized form.

  • validate sanitizes each part and compares it to the original. Any difference means the part carried disallowed or non-canonical markup, so it returns a :class:FailedResult with :attr:DISALLOWED_HTML.
  • mutate returns the sanitized text as a whole-part edit for each part that changed; unchanged parts are left untouched.

The sanitizer is powered by nh3 (the Rust ammonia library over html5ever). Because it parses input into a tree and re-serializes, it is resilient to syntactic obfuscation — mixed case (<ScRiPt>), HTML entities (javascript:), and malformed nesting are all resolved to the canonical tree before the allowlist is applied.

Precondition — HTML only. Apply this to content that is meant to be rendered as HTML. Plain text is not safe input: a stray < or > (as in 5 < 3) is HTML-escaped, which changes the text and is reported as a violation. Deciding whether content should be HTML at all is the caller's routing decision, not this validator's job.

Safe defaults, widen at your own risk. Out of the box the policy is HTML-only with a tightened URL-scheme set and inline CSS disabled. Every constructor parameter that widens the allowlist enlarges the attack surface; two are especially load-bearing:

  1. Adding foreign-content tags (svg, math, foreignObject) reopens namespace-confusion vectors that the HTML-only default avoids.
  2. Enabling inline CSS (allowed_css_properties) is only as safe as the property list you allow — see that parameter's documentation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default allowed_tags set[str] | None

The set of permitted tag names. None (default) uses nh3's vetted HTML-only default set. Passing a set replaces the default entirely rather than adding to it.

None allowed_attributes dict[str, set[str]] | None

A mapping of tag name to the set of attributes permitted on it (use "*" as the key for attributes allowed on any tag). None (default) uses nh3's per-tag default, which contains no event-handler attributes. Passing a mapping replaces the default entirely and is honored as given: if you allowlist an event handler such as onclick, it is kept — you own that choice, exactly as you do when you allowlist the javascript URL scheme or a risky tag. Widen this only for content you trust. (Inline CSS is the one exception: the style attribute is governed solely by allowed_css_properties and is dropped when that is None, regardless of this mapping.)

None allowed_url_schemes set[str] | frozenset[str]

The URL schemes permitted in URL-bearing attributes. Defaults to http, https, mailto; javascript: and data: are excluded, so they are stripped.

DEFAULT_ALLOWED_URL_SCHEMES allowed_css_properties set[str] | frozenset[str] | None

The inline-CSS properties permitted in style attributes. None (default) disables inline CSS entirely — the style attribute is removed even if you allow it in allowed_attributes. Passing a set enables inline CSS limited to those properties; nh3 also sanitizes property values (dropping url() values whose scheme is disallowed). The set is honored as given, so start from a small, vetted set of visual properties rather than allowing arbitrary ones. Avoid behavior and -moz-binding: they load script through a url() that nh3's value-level filtering does not catch, so allowlisting them re-enables a script vector.

None strip_comments bool

Whether to remove HTML comments. Defaults to True — comments can leak metadata and are not rendered content.

True link_rel str | None

The rel value forced onto <a> tags. Defaults to "noopener noreferrer", which mitigates reverse-tabnabbing. Pass None to leave rel untouched.

'noopener noreferrer' Example

from aegis import MutationGuard guard = MutationGuard("output").use(HtmlSanitizer()) result = await guard.validate("Hello") result.was_mutated True result.output 'Hello'

def __init__(
    self,
    *,
    allowed_tags: set[str] | None = None,
    allowed_attributes: dict[str, set[str]] | None = None,
    allowed_url_schemes: set[str] | frozenset[str] = DEFAULT_ALLOWED_URL_SCHEMES,
    allowed_css_properties: set[str] | frozenset[str] | None = None,
    strip_comments: bool = True,
    link_rel: str | None = "noopener noreferrer",
) -> None:
    self._tags = allowed_tags
    self._url_schemes = set(allowed_url_schemes)
    self._css_properties = set(allowed_css_properties) if allowed_css_properties is not None else None
    self._strip_comments = strip_comments
    self._link_rel = link_rel

    # A caller-supplied ``allowed_attributes`` replaces the default entirely and is
    # honored as given — the same contract ``allowed_tags`` and ``allowed_url_schemes``
    # follow. Safety comes from the safe defaults, not from silently overriding an
    # explicit request. Three cases:
    # 1. A tag→attributes mapping is kept as passed. If a caller allowlists an event
    #    handler such as ``onclick`` it stays — their explicit choice, no different
    #    from allowlisting the ``javascript`` scheme or the ``iframe`` tag.
    # 2. ``style`` is the one exception, and it is parameter precedence rather than an
    #    override: inline CSS is controlled solely by ``allowed_css_properties``, so
    #    when that is None (CSS off) a ``style`` entry here is dropped. Otherwise nh3
    #    with no property filter would allow *every* CSS property, silently enabling
    #    unfiltered inline CSS the caller did not ask for. Matched case-insensitively,
    #    since HTML attribute names are.
    # 3. ``None`` passes straight to nh3, whose per-tag default contains no event
    #    handlers.
    if allowed_attributes is not None and self._css_properties is None:
        self._attributes: dict[str, set[str]] | None = {
            tag: {attr for attr in attrs if attr.lower() != "style"} for tag, attrs in allowed_attributes.items()
        }
    else:
        self._attributes = allowed_attributes

async def validate(self, view: ContentView, metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None) -> ValidationResult:
    """Report whether every part is already in its sanitized form.

    Each part is sanitized independently and compared to the original. We
    compare against the sanitized form rather than trying to recognize "bad"
    markup directly: the allowlist is the only arbiter of safety, so anything
    the sanitizer would change — a disallowed tag, a dropped attribute, or even
    benign normalization such as closing an open tag — is treated as a
    violation to repair. This favors safety over precision; for a mutation
    validator the cost of a benign-normalization "false" failure is nil, since
    ``mutate`` simply emits the already-canonical form.

    Args:
        view: The content under inspection. Each item is treated as an
            independent HTML fragment.
        metadata: Surrounding agent context. Unused — the sanitizer governs
            markup only, never the meaning of the prose.

    Returns:
        :class:`PassedResult` when every part equals its sanitized form,
        otherwise a :class:`FailedResult` with ``error_code``
        :attr:`DISALLOWED_HTML`. The ``details`` mapping carries only safe
        summaries — ``changed_parts`` and the summed ``original_length`` /
        ``sanitized_length`` — never the raw markup, which could contain an
        XSS payload or an embedded secret.
    """
    changed_parts = 0
    original_length = 0
    sanitized_length = 0
    for part in view.items:
        sanitized = self._clean(part.value)
        if sanitized != part.value:
            changed_parts += 1
            original_length += len(part.value)
            sanitized_length += len(sanitized)

    if changed_parts:
        details: dict[str, Any] = {
            "changed_parts": changed_parts,
            "original_length": original_length,
            "sanitized_length": sanitized_length,
        }
        return FailedResult(
            error_code=self.DISALLOWED_HTML,
            error_message="Content contains disallowed or non-canonical HTML markup.",
            details=details,
        )
    return PassedResult()

Only parts that actually change are addressed; an unchanged part is left alone, which keeps the edit set minimal and lets the engine report was_mutated=False when nothing needed fixing.

async def mutate(
    self,
    view: ContentView,
    metadata: GuardMetadata | None = None,
    validation_failure: FailedResult | None = None,
) -> list[ItemEdit]:
    """Return the sanitized form of each part that is not already clean.

    Only parts that actually change are addressed; an unchanged part is left
    alone, which keeps the edit set minimal and lets the engine report
    ``was_mutated=False`` when nothing needed fixing.

    The output is safe to re-validate: feeding it back through ``validate``
    yields :class:`PassedResult`, because sanitizing already-sanitized content
    is a no-op (``clean(clean(x)) == clean(x)``). This fixed-point property is
    what lets the mutation path be trusted, and is enforced by the test suite.

    Args:
        view: The content to repair.
        metadata: Surrounding agent context. Unused.
        validation_failure: The failure from ``validate``. Unused — ``mutate``
            recomputes the sanitized form directly rather than depending on the
            detection details.

    Returns:
        One :class:`ItemEdit` per changed part, addressed by part id.
    """
    edits: list[ItemEdit] = []
    for part in view.items:
        sanitized = self._clean(part.value)
        if sanitized != part.value:
            edits.append(ItemEdit(part.id, sanitized))
    return edits
